speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Secretary of State of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF UNIVERSAL DECLARATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to inform all Members of this House that today is Human Rights Day and marks the 39th anniversary of the universal Declaration of Human Rights. This historic document on basic rights and fundamental freedoms was proclaimed on December 10, 1948, by the United Nations. Its philosophy of equality and personal dignity symbolized a new era in human understanding and tolerance. The member nations that signed the declaration in 1948 voiced their united support for individual liberty in all countries throughout the world.
For our part, we in Canada have continued to stress the importance of these principles within our own borders with a distinctly Canadian vision of a fair and harmonious society.

The 1960 Canadian Bill of Rights affirmed the privileges which all Canadians enjoy as citizens of this country. Bearing the signature of the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker, this monument to freedom which we hold so dearly states, among other things: " . . . in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race,
national origin, colour, religion or sex, the . . . human rights and fundamental freedoms ... ".

Our Canadian Human Rights Act came into being in 1977, followed by the Constitution Act of 1982. This encompassed the social principles of our Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, a statement in support of human dignity and equality that is the envy of many of our neighbours worldwide.
On December 1, I tabled in this House the Canadian Multicultural Act. When passed, this historic Bill will confirm the constitutional freedom of all Canadians of whatever origin to preserve and enhance their multicultural heritage and to share it with others. It will recognize that all of us are equal participants in our society, thereby reinforcing both our Canadian identity and the unity of this country.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has also heralded civil rights on a world-wide scale. The position we have taken against the injustices we see in South Africa, in Central America, and in a number of other regions of the world vividly attests to our firm determination to restore the kind of climate where all nations of the world will be able to feel like true equals.
[DOT] (UIO)

Another example of the Government's commitment to human rights lies in its plans to establish the International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development as jointly announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Landry). This centre's important mandate will be to uphold human rights and strengthen democratic institutions by means of international co-operation.
International Humans Rights Day is a time for recalling the millions in the world who are denied their basic rights. It is also an occasion for solemn reflection, for some through prayer, for others through giving thanks, for the blessings we enjoy in Canada where human rights for everyone is a central pillar of our society's structure.

As Canada grew to maturity, its citizens displayed ever increasing openmindedness in mutual respect for one another. But we still have some way to go because it is always possible to improve the situation. Given the understanding which has

December 10, 1987
Statements by Ministers
developed between the people and the Government of Canada, I firmly believe that the principles underlying our hopes are that much stronger. Indeed, cultural or racial origins must not stand as obstacles to the free expression of fundamantal rights.

Allow me to conclude by quoting from the introduction to the Multiculturalism Act a week ago. It states:
.. . The Government calls upon all citizens to make a renewed commitment to the principles of equality, diversity, and community and to continue the great task of building their homeland into a free and united country that will continue to be a symbol of hope in a fractious, turbulent world .. . The proposed Act should reinforce Canada's stature among the nations of the world, adding another page to the country's long record as a leader in matters relating to human and civil rights.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read the text of the Minister's statement which I received about an hour ago, and I have listened carefully in the hopes that it might be amended. On an occasion as important as International Human Rights Day, I am frankly disappointed that he would limit himself to painting such a rosy picture of human rights in Canada and, in a sense, publicize or promote his own legislative program when the world is in such agony and chaos. Instead of addressing the problems facing our native people, or the inequality affecting women, or the problems of discrimination faced by visible minorities, the disabled and handicapped, he has reviewed and rehashed generalities with which I am sure we all agree. I wonder if the Minister wrote the statement himself.
The Minister spoke about the Multiculturalism Bill, and of course we have all supported the multiculturalism concept for decades. Yet I would have liked him to have told us what it actually achieves. What does it do, for example, about racism and discrimination?
The Minister passed over the world's problems in several sentences, yet at this very hour burning issues exist. Let us take just one example, that of Haiti, where a brutal military regime has savaged its population for several years and sponsored or condoned death squads which have been murdering citizens lining up for an election. The election had to be cancelled for that reason and that Government has had the audacity to announce today that it is trying to call illegal elections for January 17. That is just one of many tragic examples of international problems. On a day of such importance and such solemnity as International Human Rights Day, I am disappointed that the Minister has not risen to the occasion and discussed with us the problems, instead of shovelling self-serving and self-congratulatory propaganda of sweetness and light for the Government.
Perhaps he would like to deal with the real human rights issues here in Canada. What about the failure to appoint a commissioner from the Atlantic region to the Canadian Human Rights Commission? What about the slow pace of dealing with human rights cases before that commission, some reputedly taking as long as a year to a year and a half or even two years? What about the failure to deal with the human
rights concerns of our native people? What about the aboriginal land claims? What about the way in which we deal with our native people in our system of justice? What about the human rights problems facing our native people with respect to housing? What about the problems faced by our native people with respect to medical care? What about youth programs? We know so many young people in the native communities are struggling to find meaning in life. What about the basic right to life? What about the fact that our native people have a higher mortality rate than others in Canada, particularly for their children? What about human rights issues in this country?
On International Human Rights Day, I was pleased that the Minister recognized the occasion but I have to ask him, on a day of this importance, can you not get serious?

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF UNIVERSAL DECLARATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I rise on behalf of the NDP to add my voice to that of the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) and the Official Opposition spokesman in recognition of the thirty-ninth anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. This day marks the culmination of the recognition of a new ideal among nations in a world where, only a century before, slavery and the attitude that supported it were pervasive.
It is because of this new ideal that we have a better world, but not a perfect world. Even now, in the glow of glasnost, Jews plead for Russian refuseniks and Afghans for their land. In Haiti the people struggle for a blood-free vote. In southern Africa, El Salvador, Nicaragua and Guatemala human rights lay victim to local tyranny and foreign conflicts. In Iran, Pakistan and elsewhere we see that religious intolerance is still a powerful force for suppression.
We in Canada, as the Minister says, can look with pride upon a nation striving to become a new model for understanding among an increasing diversity of people. As we increasingly reflect the many peoples of the world in our own citizenship, we are asked to become an increasingly powerful voice on the world stage for equality, justice and freedom. Whether it be in southern Africa, Central America or elsewhere, we must be sure that our voice will be heard above the cacophony of national or big power interests which tempt compromise. In our own land the recognition in legislation of the multiculturalism of our land is not enough unless equality is absolutely assured.
On this thirty-ninth anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, let us not forget that, as we celebrate Meech Lake, we still have not dealt with the limits on equality presented in our Charter of Rights by the override clause. Those of us who have supported Meech Lake and those of us who look upon Canada as a multicultural nation insist that the first priority, as the provinces and the federal Government deliberate about the next constitutional change, be the elimination of the that clause which says to too many of us
December 10, 1987

who are not of English or French descent that we are not quite equal if there is a need for compromise for some purpose.
Let us also recognize that increasingly those of us who looked with hope upon the Human Rights Commissions of the federal Government and the provinces see now that they have virtually deserted us. When it takes not days, not weeks, but years all too often for complaints of discrimination to be processed by provincial human rights commissions or the federal Human Rights Commission, it suggests to many that we are willing to move too slowly on something which should have been completed long ago and for which there was so much hope not too long ago.
We join in celebration. We are proud of the contribution that Canada has made. We are pleased by the changes which make this country more representative of the world's population, but we cannot sit down on this day satisfied that we have achieved perfection domestically or internationally. We have done well, but we have much more to do.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
That this House condemn the government for its failure to allow an adequate period of review prior to the signing of a highly complex trade agreement with the United States pn January 2. 1988 and, as a result, this House calls upon the government to seek an extension of the January 2nd deadline by at least 60 days.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we are just three short weeks away from signing what has been described as the most significant economic agreement in the history of the relationships between Canada and the United States. That description is one which my Party shares. This deal is indeed very significant, if not quite comparable to the Magna Carta which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would like to suggest from time to time in his highly exaggerated rhetoric, and will have an immense impact on the lives of Canadians, not only for the rest of this century but into the next century as well.
Yet, as serious as this is, the incredible fact remains that the Parliament of Canada has not yet seen the final text. This is absolutely outrageous.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext: Shame, shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
The Conservative Government and the United States administration agreed to the elements of this proposal in the first weekend of October. We were assured at that time that the people of Canada and their representatives here in the Parliament of Canada would have a final legal text within a matter of weeks. Weeks turned into months and it will be more than two months after that promise was made that a final text will be presented.
We are now told that tomorrow the Government of Canada will release publicly a 250-page agreement with over 1,200 pages of tariff tables for the people outside of Parliament and the Parliament of Canada finally to consider in detail. In terms of the parliamentary agenda leading into the Christmas period, that means that an agreement of this immense complexity and seriousness will have to be discussed and debated, according to the Government's proposed schedule, for only five days, the five sitting days of next week.
On behalf of all the members of my Party and, I am sure, of Canadians from coast to coast, this is not a democratic process but a mockery of the democratic process.

December 10, 1987
Supply

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister, regrettably, is still determined to sign this deal on a schedule imposed and proposed by the United States of America. The January 2 date was not decided upon as a consequence of a Canadian initiative even though the impact of this deal will be much more significant on the lives of Canadians than it will be on the lives of Americans for the obvious reason that their society and economy is so much larger than ours. Even though the consequences are much more horrendous from our point of view, and positive from the Government's point of view, the Government has accepted the January 2 deadline which was proposed by the United States.
Even the Conservative Chairman of the Committee on External Affairs and International Trade which looked into this accord in the past few weeks, without the final wording of course, has said that it would be "absolutely silly", to use his words, for his committee to consider the final text until some time in the new year.
Surely when a government proposes such a massive change in Canada-U.S. relations there is an obligation to ensure that the democratic rights of Canadians to consider this deal are honoured. If it was absolutely silly to think that the committee could consider the final wording of this text in a matter of days, it is absolutely silly and irresponsible for the Government to expect the Parliament of Canada to do so in a matter of a few days.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
For once the Government should act in a responsible and serious manner. It has an obligation to live up to the implications of the serious agreement which it has signed. It has an obligation to give Parliament, the provinces and, most of all, the people of Canada, the facts on which they are supposed to make a judgment.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative majority decided that the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade would be on the road for less than two weeks. Dozens of private citizens and groups have been unable to make presentations before the Committee. Only a few groups and individuals have had a chance to explain their concerns to the Parliamentary Committee. Day after day, NDP Members on the Committee moved to have the hearings opened to the public. Day after day, they moved to give ordinary citizens a chance to express their views, and day after day, the Conservative majority voted against this democratic opening up of the consultation process.
Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives did not want a democratic process. They merely wanted to give the impression it was democratic. That is typical of this Government.
Today's debate is not about the substance of the Agreement. We may have a debate on that Monday, at least I hope so.
Today, our subject is the need for a real, informed debate in this country. We are talking about the democratic rights of the Canadian people. Whether Canadians are for or against the Agreement, most Canadians would like to see the details of the Agreement. They want a chance to judge the Agreement with all the facts.
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians share our concern about fundamental changes in our political, social and economic life. The status of our relations with the United States is crucial for Canadians, especially for our trade relations.
Today we are each other's principal economic partner, and that will remain so. However, Mr. Speaker, as a nation, we are masters in our own house and we want it to stay that way. The Conservatives must understand this fact. All Canadians understand the basic reality of our economic and foreign policies and their impact on our relations with the United States. All Canadians understand as well that in business terms, a healthy relationship with the United States is of vital importance to our economy, our communities and our jobs. That is why we are so concerned about the impact this trade agreement will have, whether on energy, agriculture or regional equity. All these concerns are central to our economy and our way of life. In all these areas, Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives have sacrificed our sovereignty. That is the truth.
On Monday I will outline at length the New Democratic Party opposition to very specific parts of the deal. Today, I simply want to note some specific matters of concern in a discussion that is fundamentally about the democratic process.
One must ask, why this particular deal? Why are we making major concessions on the control of our decision-making in energy, on our right to retain control over business enterprises to ensure that they stay in Canadian hands in almost every sector. Why are we making major concessions that will negatively affect the agricultural sector, the manufacturing sector and particularly will have a negative effect over the capacity of our western provinces to become industrialized and not simply remain resource exporters?
The Deputy Minister of Finance has already announced major changes affecting our capacity to have just and equitable regional development programs. All of these elements are found in this deal. Why is the Government doing this? I hope that either today or in Monday's debate these questions will be faced head on.
When the Prime Minister first proposed this, we had a $20 billion surplus in trade with the United States in our commercial exchange. We were doing quite well in trade with the United States. It is true that from the time the Prime Minister announced this the United States has taken negative actions against some of our key exports which, incidentally, were supposed to be going in duty-free already.
December 10, 1987

In spite of those actions, most of which were unfair and totally unwarranted, even today the monthly trade figures for October show that we had a surplus in our merchandise trade with the United States of $840 million. So far this year we have had a trade surplus with the United States of $10.1 billion without this deal.
I say, as a Canadian and a New Democrat, that we are a confident and competent people. Whatever the domain of activity, whether it is the arts, athletic activity, or business activity, during the last 25 years in particular I believe that Canadians are second to none in the world. In terms of our ability to compete with the United States of America, we have never been in a better position. In sector after sector we are winning the competition with the United States already.
I want to remind the Conservatives who are embarking upon this historic mess that already 95 per cent of our exports into the United States are duty free or at a level of duty or tariff of 5 per cent or less. We are doing well in competition. We are not confronted by significant tariff barriers for most of our exports to the United States.
The Government reminds us that the Americans took unfair actions in some parts of our economy. We all noted that and objected to it. The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) promised that the Conservative Government would move "to get unfair U.S. laws changed", and said that we had to have guaranteed access to the United States markets. The Conservatives went after a dispute settlement mechanism which the Minister for International Trade and other spokespersons for the Government said would give us this guaranteed access. They got no such thing. There is a tribunal that does not have the authority to change U.S. laws.

speechtext: Or Canadian laws.

Or Canadian laws. I say to the Member opposite that it was not our agenda, it was the Conservatives who promised to get us guaranteed access to the U.S. markets. After making so many sacrifices, they did not even get that.
If we are winning in our trade competition with the United States, whether it is in shakes and shingles, softwood, tubular steel, pork or any other part of our trade, the U.S. Congress will have exactly the same powers to pass unfair laws against us as they had before this agreement.

speechtext:
The Member says that is wrong. I hope he can prove it. If he can, it will be the first time he has done so in the House.
Unless there is a fundamental change in the nature of the dispute settlement mechanism, the constitutional right of the U.S. Congress to take action against us when we win the

competition will remain in place. The Government got nothing, having given away so much on the part of the people of Canada.
Not only did it get nothing out of what was stated to be its central goal in these negotiations, but our prairie farmers, in this case, the grain exporters, thought that if we had this locked in trade agreement with the United States, at least they should be protected from massive American subsidies in grain exports when they export directly to countries in which we have had traditional markets, whatever other limitations in the agreement.
Our grain exporters are the most efficient producers of grain in the world and are quite prepared to meet honest competition. But the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) tried to justify the continuity of these subsidies by saying: "Oh, these were from a pre-existing program established by the U.S. Congress". It is a pre-existing program that will still be applicable, that can still use the massive resources of the U.S. treasury against our agricultural sector which is effective and competitive, and I say, once again, the Government sold out the interests of our grain producers.
The right of Canadians to export processed products as opposed to unprocessed products is something we in this Party have maintained as a goal. We have wanted this, particularly for the development of western Canada; not to be hewers of wood and drawers of water, not to go for the quick buck fix so characteristic of the Tories. We wanted the right to maintain as a nation the sovereign control over resource development to whatever level of finished processing before we export it.
There was a preliminary decision by GATT against a very important part of the British Columbia economy, the export of processed fish. According to news reports about the change in the wording of this agreement, incredibly enough, this Conservative Government is prepared to sacrifice this right. It has-and we will see if they got it-maintained the right for the east coast fisheries to ensure that we can export processed fish without having action taken against us by the U.S., but it has completely capitulated in terms of the interests of British Columbia, and we find it totally unacceptable.
To give one more example, late yesterday afternoon I had incredible news presented to me by a document produced by the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association of Canada, which up to this point had been supporting this deal on a tentative basis. It has now unequivocally withdrawn its support. Why? Interestingly enough, when it saw the first wording on the weekend of October 3 and October 4, the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association, like the New Democratic Party, opposed this deal in this particular instance because of its impact on the automotive sector. It went to work to try at least to persuade the Government to increase the North American content in automotive production.

December 10, 1987
Supply
I remind Conservatives Members we are talking about 65,000 direct jobs in automotive parts alone, not considering the indirect jobs. The Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association wanted the Government to at least raise the North American content from 50 per cent to 60 per cent in this agreement. I learned yesterday that the American side had agreed to this, that the Americans saw this could be like the original Auto Pact, if it applied equitably to both sides.
If we consider competition from other parts of the world, both Canada and the United States could benefit from increasing the North American content provisions from 50 per cent to 60 per cent. It would have been beneficial to Canadians, and the Americans concluded it would have been beneficial to the Americans as well. Incredibly enough, I learned yesterday that it was the Canadian side in the negotiations that said no to this. The Canadian spokesperson said this was not in the Government's interests. So we have the incredible situation that the Government gave away the enforcement mechanism of tariff imposition to enforce the Auto Pact, the Canadian Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association arguing for some improvement, at least raising North American content from 50 per cent to 60 per cent, the American side agreeing with this and the Canadian side turning it down. I say this is disgusting behaviour and totally unacceptable to Canadians wherever they may live.
As I said at the outset of my comments on this motion, although I referred to a few of the details of the resolution today, the debate is fundamentally about process, about the denial of a serious opportunity to Canadians to consider the impact of this major proposal in their lives. When so many significant groups representing all walks of life have indicated their concern about having the opportunity to learn, to understand and to comment upon the agreement, the Government has an obligation, in our view, to respond fully and to facilitate such a debate and discussion. It is a denial of democracy not to give the Canadian people an opportunity to fully examine this deal.
The committee studying this proposal, as all Members of the House know, went simply to a handful of cities across the country from Vancouver to St. John's. It obviously heard from some people in those hearings. However, I ask, what about the people and groups who were denied the opportunity to speak to the committee either to give their views or to obtain information? Even given the committee's own democratic decision not to advertise, many groups and individuals in all these communities tried to appear before the committee and were frustrated in their attempts.
An anti-poverty organization in Fredericton, womens' groups in Edmonton, a textile firm in Montreal, seniors' groups in Toronto, all were denied their right to be heard on this important matter which affects their lives and the lives of all other Canadians. In Manitoba over 30 different groups wanted to appear before the committee and could not. In Charlottetown, the coalition against this deal was forced to hold its own hearings because it was denied access to the
committee. A British Columbia coalition of 43 groups was given only a 30 minute hearing. That worked out roughly to 20 seconds each. I repeat, this is not a democratic process. It makes a travesty of democratic process.
Other groups which did get to appear, particularly in Atlantic Canada, gave the deal only qualified or lukewarm support. Many said they wanted to see the final text before making up their minds. The Economic Council of Newfoundland, the Halifax Board of Trade and the Atlantic Chamber of Commerce gave the deal what could at best be described as lukewarm support. The Yellowknife Chamber of Commerce said the Government is trying to sell free trade and not educate Canadians as to its content. The Prince Edward Island seafood processors complained of what they described as political manipulation.
The Prime Minister and the Government have to be seen to be doing more precisely what they are doing. What they are up to is not presenting a democratic process. What they are up to is railroading a deal through Parliament, disregarding the whole democratic process of this country. They are doing it in a way with which we totally and fundamentally disagree.
While the Canadian Prime Minister refuses to give Canadians adequate time to assess this measure, it is worth noting that in the United States members of the U.S. Congress will have a minimum of three months to consider its impact. Our Parliament does not again reconvene after next week until after the January 2 deadline. While Canadian families will be celebrating with their loved ones, friends and neighbours, and while they are enjoying themselves during the Christmas period, this Government will be busy signing away the country's control over its own future. Beginning the new year by signing away the control of the country without allowing the country a chance to study this deal is absolutely unacceptable to the New Democratic Party and the people of Canada.
Just last week the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in the House:
January 2 is a day of no great significance to Canadians or to the House of
Commons.
He was right when he said that. It remains true today. But the Prime Minister has refused to act on what the logical implications of that announcement are. If January 2 has no great significance to the people of Canada and to the Parliament of Canada, why doesn't the Prime Minister put an end to January 2 as the deadline?

Mr. Speaker, I thank members of the Government and others for giving me the extended time. I will not abuse that privilege.
December 10, 1987

I want to conclude by saying that the Prime Minister does owe the people of Canada the right to thoroughly look at, to understand in all its complexity, what he has described as the most important economic deal in the history of relations between our two countries. There is nothing magic and there is nothing of significance about January 2. We need as a people at least the amount of time the Americans have to assess the impact of this proposed arrangement on our lives. Canadians want, Canadians deserve and Canadians should have the democratic right to a real debate on the facts. The deadline of January 2 must be extended.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened today with great interest to the leader of the socialist Party in Canada. There are a couple of areas in his speech with which I agree wholeheartedly. One is that Canadians are good, they are competitive. They work well and they are able to compete in this world today. 1 agree with him wholeheartedly, they are. That is what this agreement is all about. There is no question that we in the Progressive Conservative Party and the Government of Canada have great faith in our workers and our competitive position within the world. We can compete with the best.
We are following a process which started after the Second World War when tariffs dropped from an average of 40 per cent on a myriad of items to an average of 9 per cent on a few selected items. What has happened to this Canada in that period of time, Mr. Speaker? We have become a stronger country, a more sovereign country and a more affluent society. Prosperity has followed. This is just the natural progression following on those reductions in tariffs to get an open trading agreement, and not only with the United States. I am sure we will have some good progress in the current negotiations that are going on under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade in Geneva today.
My friend from Oshawa fears a great American takeover. The economy of his riding is generated by one of the finest automobile manufacturing operations in the world, namely, General Motors. He fears the American investment and he fears the Americans coming. He keeps saying around the country that we are going to be the fifty-first. Yet he welcomes with open arms $2 billion of investment by General Motors in his riding. That is welcomed with open arms. He does not call for an investigation or a review of that investment, not at all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE

As I was saying before I was so dramatically interrupted, the consultations that we have had in the last number of years with Canadians on the free trade negotiations are unprecedented. Most legitimate, if not all legitimate studies done outside of Government have recommended that we enter into these trade negotiations. It was most important that this be done to protect and enlarge our markets. From the time the negotiations were begun, we have had those consultations and they have allowed us to enter into a two-way dialogue with business, labour, consumers, and with the provinces. The core of the system of consultation has been the International Trade Advisory Committee system to provide a two-way flow of information and advice between the Government and the private sector.
Under the distinguished chairmanship of Mr. Walter Light, bringing together more than 40 leaders from business, labour, consumer groups, and academia, the ITAC, the International Trade Advisory Committee, has concerned itself with broad matters relating to international trade access and marketing. It has made valuable recommendations to the free trade agreement negotiation process.
Complementing the work of ITAC are 15 sectoral advisory groups of international trade, SAGITs. The SAGITs represent a broad cross-section of the Canadian economy. For the record, I wish to cover the sectors that are represented. There is agriculture, food and beverage; fish and fish products; minerals and metals; energy products and services; chemicals and petrochemicals; forest products; industrial, marine and rail equipment; automotive and aerospace; textiles, footwear and leather; apparel and fur; consumer and household products; communications, computer equipment and services; financial services; general services; arts and cultural industries.
The SAGITs were all selected in close co-operation and consultation with various national trade groups, provincial Governments, and labour. Both the ITACs and the SAGITs were provided regular briefings on the state of the negotiations by the senior negotiators of the trade negotiation office, and had the opportunity to formulate recommendations directly to the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney). More than 150 meetings of the sectoral advisory committees and their working groups have been held over the past 18 months. We asked for advice, we listened to it, and we acted on it.
Over and above the formal SAGIT consultations there have been dozens of briefings and consultations by officials from the trade negotiations office with all segments of the private sector. Recently the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has held extensive consultations-

Apart from close consultation with the private sector, the Government undertook to work closely and co-operatively with the provinces. The First Ministers were briefed and consulted regularly as the negotiations progressed. They received briefings with slide presentations on every detail of the agreement. Typifying the co-operative spirit which this Government has fostered, through the Meech Lake Accord and other federal-provincial co-operative endeavours-even our Liberal friend from the Province of Ontario stated that the new attitude is very positive for Canada-the First Ministers were kept fully apprised, not through personal briefings but by a detailed network of contacts at the senior officials level.
In fact, since the negotiations began, we have held approximately nine First Ministers' meetings where the free trade agreement was the single agenda item; three First Ministers' Conferences where free trade was extensively discussed, most recently in Toronto on November 26 and 27. There have been 19 full day committee meetings of the senior officials forum, the continuing committee on trade negotiations, and scores of working group meetings on every subject of the free trade agreement. More than 500 documents have been shared with the provinces. In addition, provincial trade Ministers and designated Ministers have met with the Minister for International Trade on several occasions to review the free trade issues. No previous Government has involved the provinces so extensively in such a comprehensive process of consultations and information sharing.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, over the last hour or so I have listened with some interest to the presentations by both the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) and the Parliamentary Secretary. relations firms his Government has hired, but by the reality of what has taken place in this country on the issue and what Canadians are saying about it.
Let us start with January 2. That is a very important date. It is not insignificant, as the Prime Minister said. Under a parliamentary form of Government, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) exchanges instruments with another country he commits us to a course of action. It is not the same for the President. He is restrained by the obligation to have congressional concurrence. When our Prime Minister signifies his intent to enter into this particular arrangement on January 2, he is committing Canada to that course of action. That is not insignificant.
The one thing which has become very clear in this debate, from whatever source, is that this is not a trade deal. It has elements of trade but the principles tabled on October 4 go way beyond the conventional trade negotiations conducted between countries. They go way beyond anything in the common market today. They deal with matters which no other group of nations has ever tried to negotiate or come to an arrangement on. They go into areas of control of our domestic economy way beyond anything attempted before, control of our energy sector-

speechtext:
-investment, cultural arrangements, and service industries. Those areas of such incredible concern were not forecast in any announcement by the Government. They were not given any kind of preliminary airing in this Parliament. Yet they were part of a deal arrived at in Washington in a sort of finger liken' good fried chicken dinner between the respective negotiators. All of a sudden we found we do not have a trade deal, we have a form of sovereignty association, economic union, and economic integration which goes way beyond anything attempted in the past. So for the Hon. Member to cite studies to demonstrate that there has already been full and adequate discussion misses the point.
The point is this agreement was not included in any of those studies. A North American energy policy was not part of any forecast that the Government provided. In fact, when two Ministers, one from Prince Edward Island and the other from Manitoba, were directly asked about that, they both said clearly that the Government did not even include the provinces in those discussions. Whatever consultations did take place, there were a lot of hidden cards in the deck which were not revealed even behind closed doors.
In addition, the Parliamentary Secretary made a historical gaff. He said this agreement is in line with successive government efforts since the 1940s to reduce trade barriers. No other Government in that period of time ever put forward the proposal that we sign a comprehensive commercial trade and economic arrangement with the U.S. There have been sectoral discussions. There have been reductions in tariffs brought about as a consequence of international negotiations, not

bilateral negotiations. This is the first time since 1911 that any Canadian Government has wilfully decided to initiate negotiations on a comprehensive trade arrangement. That has nothing to do with historical continuity. This deal breaks that continuity and, furthermore, goes against the wisdom of history which shows that we were able to achieve reduction of tariff barriers without surrendering control over large parts of our economy.
One of the distinct advantages of securing trade liberalization through the international system is that you can do it without having to surrender autonomy over your own economy. The rules of subsidy under GATT are very different from the rules of subsidy established by the Americans. They did not concern themselves with regional development policies or cultural issues. That was not part of the international trade regime, but this is. The Hon. Member wants facts. That is a historical fact and the Hon. Member is wrong in what he said as a result. He did not state the facts properly.
Let us talk about these consultations that went on. He talked about SAGITs and industrial groups. During the course of the committee's travels across the country I had occasion to ask the National Anti-Poverty Organization whether it was consulted. No, it was not. Was the National Farmers Union consulted? No, it was not. Were the churches consulted? No, they were not. Were women's organizations consulted? No, they were not. In other words, a large part of the Canadian population was excluded from those consultations.
What the Hon. Member was really describing was an elite process. Consultations were confined primarily to spokespersons or advocates of those who want a free trade arrangement. They did not include a broad spectrum of Canadian society. When he tries to make the case that consultation is already taking place, yes, consultation among friends but not among the broad population.
It is interesting to ask who was the chief agricultural representative appearing in front of that committee. It was the spokesman for Cargill! Hardly what you would call a representative of the grain economy in western Canada. That company certainly has a right to be heard but it certainly does not represent the kind of broad-based pool and co-operative farm movement on the Prairies.
On the other side of the border, who was the chief advisor on agriculture to the Secretary of the Treasury and the Chief Trade Negotiator? It was the former president of Cargill. They got it both ways. They locked up the consultation process in one company. So when we talk about consultation, we have to ask who, and for what interest?

speechtext: Be honest.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member talked about a wide range of studies which were produced to provide support for the trade deal. Let us look at those studies for a moment. Where do they come from? Who did them? What was in them? What did the Macdonald Commission report, the Government's Bible, have to say? It said there are two kinds of
major trade issues, tariff and non-tariff barriers. The nontariff barriers can only be handled, says the report, by getting an exemption from U.S. trade laws. In other words, the primary criteria established by the Macdonald Commission, has not been met by this agreement. To cite that report as proof that somehow this agreement has a wealth of evidence behind it simply ignores the studies themselves.
What about the famous Economic Council report which has been waved in the face of countless House of Commons sessions by the Prime Minister to prove that 350,000 jobs will be created. The Economic Council based its study on the premise that countervail and anti-dumping laws would no longer apply to Canada. Furthermore, it did not include the service industry which accounts for 70 percent of jobs. The arrangement that has been negotiated does not include exemptions from countervail and anti-dumping and does include the service sector. In other words, the study is irrelevant and useless.
The point is that we have to talk about the deal. All that went before is only prologue. We have to talk about the specifics of the deal. What has the Government done to enable large numbers of Canadians to gain information about the arrangement and to ensure that when Canadians were consulted they would be listened to and responded to? There is no point in undertaking consultation if it is a one-way street, if it does not complete the circle. If there is no response from the Government it is only a cynical, crass attempt to manipulate public opinion. In genuine consultation people are responded to.
What have we achieved with this arrangement? When the elements of the agreement were tabled on October 4 we were promised that there would be a final text in a matter of a few days, in a couple of weeks at most. We are still awaiting that final text. The Government expects Canadians to give their opinions on something they have not yet seen. That would give Jonathan Swift a wonderful subject for satire. It is too bad that he is not alive to day to listen to the Parliamentary Secretary speak. He would have a new rendition of Gulliver's Travels. Let us go out and consult, they say, but we will not tell them what we are consulting about because we do not yet have the final text.
We understand that there were problems in the second round of negotiations. We understood that there were pressures. Why could the Government not be honest and say so? Why could it not just say that the October 4 document was incomplete and had problems, that it had to go back to the bargaining table and renegotiate, that it would come back with an agreement in December and start with the fast track process? Instead, the Government maintained its charade. It launched a committee across the country without the final text.
December 10, 1987

The Member pointed to that committee with great pride. He said that we had all the consultation we could possibly stand. In fact, the majority members on that committee refused, by vote, to extend the hearings to a date when we would have a final text. They refused to open the committee by advertising in newspapers where the committee was sitting in order that people could come forward. Witnesses were pre-selected.
There have been plenty of precedents for the openness about which I have spoken. When I was a member of the Joint Committee on International Relations which studied free trade one of the most important parts of the committee's hearings was at the end of each day when the session was opened up to individual representations. It is true that sometimes we had to sit until 11 p.m. or midnight, but some days we heard 20 or 30 unsolicited Canadians who came forward to be heard. That was one of the most important parts of that committee because it gave us insight into the basic anxieties and concerns of a broad cross-section of Canadians.
This committee was deliberately refused that opportunity by the majority of Tory members on that committee. For the Hon. Member to stand in this House and say that that was a legitimate process denies what went on. It denies the fact that a parliamentary committee was restricted, limited, and circumscribed in the proper functioning of its duties. It is a fact on the record that the committee was handicapped in its work.
After 100 years of tradition in this House and centuries of tradition in the British House the whole point of having a committee is that it will be heard and that its report will be tabled in the House and responded to. The committee will report next Tuesday. Its report will contain a number of recommendations from people who spoke about how the agreement must be changed. Even those who are philosophically in favour of free trade said that it is a bad agreement and needs correction. Is the Prime Minister going to allow those corrections to take place? Is he going to give proper and due consideration to the findings of that committee?
For example, we are faced with a fundamental dilemma in that the Grocery Products Manufacturers association, the largest employer in Canada employing close to 300,000 workers, said that under this deal they may be forced out of business because, by reducing tariffs to zero, the Americans will be able to import packaged, processed, and frozen goods at a much lower cost, while in Canada we are also being required to fulfil supply management. We must remove supply management or they will be put out of business by the tariff changes. They asked the committee to do something about it. 1 am not making that up, it is the fact.
It would seem to me that a government interested in governing would recognize that it is putting at risk the whole food processing industry of Canada, to say nothing of the supply management system. That legitimate and deeply-felt concern was expressed to the committee.
Supply
Will the committee's findings on that be incorporated in the new agreement? Of course not. The Prime Minister is going to run off and sign something on January 2. He will not fulfil his proper parliamentary obligation to listen to the findings of a committee of this House. We say that the rights of Parliament are being usurped and one can find no clearer evidence of that than what I have just cited.
A very dangerous trend is being started by the Government. The constitutional arrangement was negotiated by the executive behind closed doors with no accountability to elected representatives, provincial or federal. This economic union arrangement was negotiated behind closed doors by executive bureaucrats who did not tell us what was going on. Now this Parliament is being denied the lawful and rightful functioning of its committee.
In addition to the clear and prevalent danger to the economic, social, and political arrangements of this country in the arrangement which the Prime Minister and the President will be signing on January 2, in whatever form, there is also the erosion of Parliament. The fundamental rights for proper and free discussion and for accountability are being undermined and eroded by the Government. This is the most basic contempt for this House that we have seen in generations. That is one of the most serious consequences that we face.
I would like to point out one final fact. The justification for this ramrod, choo-choo, hurry up, headless horseman approach to the trade deal has been that we must follow the American timetable of the fast track. That has been the one and only justification. Today we learned that the chairman of the Ways and Means Committee and the chairman of the Senate Finance Committee said that the agreement would not even be dealt with until June. Mr. Speaker, the fast track is in Canada and the slow track is in the United States.
The timetable has nothing to do with the American timetable in this respect. If the American legislators are saying they cannot even begin to deal with the matter until late June, would it not have been proper to ask for the kind of extension that this motion seeks? According to the American legislation, Congress has the right to grant that extension. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary that the Congress has the right to grant that extension, if requested. But the Government has not even taken the time to request it.
Once more, we see that contempt for Parliament and the complete disdain for the rights of Canadians to know what is happening and be able to understand what will be in the agreement. The Government has refused to listen and respond to their concerns, and incorporate them in the agreement itself. All the fundamental obligations of a parliamentary democratic system are being spurned, ignored and thwarted by the Government in proceeding as it has with this particular deal.

The Liberal Party was also divided on the Meech Lake Accord, an agreement that in the final instance led to national reconciliation, while the profound differences within the Liberal Party were not surprising, considering the divisive policies of this Party.
Regarding the issue before the House today, 1 would like to ask the Hon. Member first of all when the Liberal Party is going to start its campaign against free trade in Quebec. Second, I want to ask him what he thinks about the position taken by the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Bourassa, who, I would think is perfectly capable of defending the interests of Quebec and has spoken out several times in favour of the Free Trade Agreement?

Mr. Speaker, for the Hon. Member's information, we have started our campaign against the Mulroney-Reagan Agreement on economic integration of Canada and the United States. In fact, Mr. Speaker, we have had several meetings with, for instance, the groups representing farmers and the agricultural industry which are very concerned about the Conservative Government's proposal. In fact, the Quebec Government has changed its position on agriculture-that may be of particular interest to the Hon. Member-and on the textile, food, clothing and research sectors.
Representatives for these industries made representations against free trade because jobs would be lost in these sectors. This is not just a Liberal concern. It is a concern that is felt by the people of Quebec as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just prior to the speech by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) a Government Member rose in his place and referred to an article in The Globe and Mail this morning which had the
headline: "Ontario Future Rosy under Trade Pact: Province Forecast". When we saw that article we immediately called the Ontario Government to find out if the report was correct. Of course, we were told that it was not.
I now have a copy of the forecast of the Ontario Treasury Department, and I believe the Hon. Member has one as well. It states:
A single quantitative estimate of the macroeconomic impact of the proposed
Canada-U.S. trade and investment agreement is not possible. The proposed
deal covers many areas and issues-for example from tariffs to investment, to
energy, to services, to procurement, to agriculture, and to dispute settlement.
Most, if not all, do not lend themselves to summary arithmetic evaluations.
It goes on. Unfortunately, even great newspapers like The Globe and Mail badly interpret complex Government reports from time to time. Would the Hon. Member comment further on this? I noticed that Government Members took great glee in referring to this headline which is now shown to be false.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand). I think he has corrected what was clearly an attempt to provide misinformation to the House.
If one reads the actual report, one can see that the economic forecast clearly states that it will not make those kind of quantitative judgments because, as I have said, so much of what is in the agreement goes way beyond trade and into the inner workings of our economy. Therefore, the judgments that must be made are those based upon whether we will retain the ability to manage our economy.
The Ontario study itself suggests that losing control over regional development, over the energy sector and over the automobile sector would result in serious consequences. It points to one example that I think is important to illustrate. Our Party's position is not against tariff reduction. Since 1948 our Party has witnessed and has initiated substantial reductions of tariffs around the world. Members of past governments have certainly made great efforts to work out amicable trade arrangements with the Americans, the Europeans and other countries.
The fallacy in the Conservative Government's case is that it puts forward the argument that only by a comprehensive bilateral, all-encompassing economic arrangement with the United States can we secure tariff reduction. Of course, that is absolute, total nonsense. Negotiations are currently taking place in GATT to reduce tariff and non-tariff barriers, without giving away all of the sectors of our economy that are included in this agreement. Furthermore, the United States trade legislation itself has a specific requirement to negotiate the reduction of tariff barriers with Canada. In other words, we would not have to become involved in energy, investment and services. They are not part of tariff reduction.
My point is that there are other ways of bringing about whatever benefits reduced tariffs may have. The way is not to sell out the fundamental institutions of this country.

They say it bodes well for the negotiations going on now in Geneva, and if Canada and the United States could not have had had a free trade agreement, two of the largest trading partners in the world, it did not bode well for the negotiations going on in Geneva at the present time. So they were supportive and pleased to see the progress made on that agreement.
The Hon. Member talked about services. Services are the fastest growing industry in the world and the GATT, which again the Opposition loves to talk about, support and embrace wholeheartedly, felt as well that services were a very important part of the negotiations, in fact, so important that they have it on their agenda for the negotiations in Geneva as well. They felt because of this fast growing part of our economy in the world that something had to be done.
If the Hon. Member is saying we took services in under this agreement, we certainly did and we are proud of it. We are a Progressive Conservative Government. We look forward to the future. We know that services play a very important part in the world's economy today and have to be tackled, and we had the guts to do it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Parliamentary Secretary has just displayed to this House the Conservative mentality when it comes to trade negotiation. He is obviously saying that we would prefer to negotiate services through a bilateral arrangement as opposed to doing it internationally. If, as he quite correctly states, GATT is going to negotiate services, then why did we not negotiate services as part of the GATT process, where there were 95 other countries involved, where we would not give up the right of establishment, and the right of investment performance, which other GATT countries are prepared to defend?
When I was at the Uruguay Round, it was made very clear that most of the other countries in the world wanted to find some way of protecting their financial institutions and their service sectors against total takeovers from large countries like the United States. Yet this country has already given that up before we even get into that negotiation.
Supply
The fact is that the international system works because there is an ability to get a much broader bargaining base against a large powerful nation like the United States when a country can have many other countries join it in that bargaining rather than doing it one on one.
When the Parliamentary Secretary states that there is general approval, I take issue with it. Arthur Dunkel, the Secretary General of GATT, has said that the most imminent danger to the international trading system is the emergence of regional trading blocs because those regional trading blocs, similar to what is being proposed today, set up discriminatory barriers against other countries. The fundamental principle of the international system is that it is non-discriminatory. The tariff and non-tariff barriers are the same for everyone. What we are negotiating under the Canada-U.S. trade arrangement is that we will be putting up different barriers than those countries in the Pacific Rim, the Europeans, the Latin Americans, and giving preference to the Americans.
That is the fundamental flaw in the whole reasoning. In fact, the Government is contributing to the breakdown of the international trading system by proposing and promoting this evolution to regional trading blocs which will simply become large, competing, controversial, combatative trading systems, and that will destroy the international trading system which this country has for so long tried to defend and promote.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pick up on an issue which was debated earlier. It has to do with the Auto Pact. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade (Mr. McDermid), was offended when some of us on this side questioned his affection for the truth with respect to how he described the Auto Pact. Like a great many Conservative Members, and like a great many proponents of this free trade agreement, the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary characterized the Auto Pact as a free trade agreement. This has been done in my own home city by the Winnipeg Free Press, for instance. It has been done right across the west by Premier Devine and others in an attempt to create the impression that somehow there is a free trade situation in Ontario with respect to automobiles that the New Democratic Party and others are trying to prevent from happening in other parts of the country.
I ask the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, rhetorically at this point because I am the one who has the floor, how in heavens name would anyone with any self respect get up and say that the Auto Pact is a free trade agreement when he knows it involves performance guarantees, safeguards, and the invocation of tariffs if certain conditions are not met? He knows all those things. He knows that they have absolutely nothing to do with free trade.
The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary comes from Brampton. He knows there has been free trade in agricultural implements since about 1948. In the free trade relationship that exists with respect to agricultural implements, there are no tariffs, no performance guarantees, no agreements that for every combine

December 10, 1987
sold in Canada we have to make one in Canada. There are no agreements whatsoever about anything. That is free trade, which is quite different from the Auto Pact.
If the only tactic that can be employed to promote this agreement is to so falsely characterize the Auto Pact, then Hon. Members opposite are indeed desperate for an argument. The fact is that the Auto Pact is not a free trade agreement and future agreements like the Auto Pact will be impossible under this agreement. Nothing could be further from the truth than what the Conservatives, whether it be the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary or Premier Devine, the Winnipeg Free Press or anyone else, happen to be saying about the Auto Pact. I do not understand it. I find it a constant source of despair that people who I otherwise respect and have a great deal of time for, have the nerve to stand and say the kinds of things they do. It is just beyond me.
The motion has to do with the timeframe in which this is all happening. The motion the New Democratic Party has moved could not be more reasonable. We are calling upon the Government not to sign the agreement on January 2 but to seek an extension of the January 2 date by at least 60 days. What could be more reasonable than for the Government to ask of its counterparts in the United States that the appropriate time for due parliamentary process in Canada be provided? We will probably have the text tomorrow. The House will likely adjourn next week and the deal will be signed January 2. Neither this House, Canadians, nor the committee charged with looking at it will have anything that remotely approaches the appropriate amount of time.
I recall when the former Liberal Government brought in an energy omnibus Bill which dealt with so many things, the Official Opposition at that time, the Conservatives, rose up in righteous indignation and tied this place up with the ringing of the bells for much longer than we will have to consider this agreement after we have the text. What has happened in the meantime to the parliamentary conscience of the Conservative Party in giving Parliament an opportunity to consider matters that are before it? One of the complaints against the energy omnibus bill was that it included too much. We did not have enough time to look at everything.
What could be more of an omnibus situation than the agreement we have before us which deals with almost every economic thing you could think of concerning Canada, yet we will get to debate the matter for only five days?

But it is not yet the United States. In this country we have a parliamentary system of Government and that means Parliament has to have its say before things are signed, not after. Congress has its say after things are signed but Congress has power after things are signed. Congress can say yes or no. In Canada the executive and legislative dimensions of Government are one in the sense that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) controls the House of Commons.
The Hon. Member is saying to us, "Well, Parliament will get to consider the implementing legislation". But he knows that there are 210 seats in his pocket. It is absolutely ridiculous. I wish people would stop making such uncritical comparisons between the American system of Government and the Canadian system. There is a difference between our two systems of Government.
The parliamentary system should be respected before our Prime Minister commits the country to an agreement between the United States and Canada, which will be quite different than what Ronald Reagan will be doing when he signs the agreement, because he will be creating the context in which he can then present it to Congress. But that is not what our Prime Minister will be doing. He will be signing the agreement. When it comes down to the real agreement, it will be Congress on the American side that signs the agreement with Canada. The Congress will sign it with the Prime Minister who will already have signed it on January 2. That is why what is happening here is one of the most enormous crimes against democracy that you can imagine, Mr. Speaker, and that is why we have moved this motion.
I take it my time has run out. I look forward to resuming this debate after Question Period.

SECURITY PROCEDURES AT AIRPORTS-CHECKING OF AIR FREIGHT SHIPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week my colleague, the Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane), brought to the attention of the House, through a committee, problems with airport security. Although the Government has made many significant improvements and innovations to airport security across Canada, two of my constituents who work in this industry brought to my attention some problems with airport security procedures.
Screening and control of small package delivery companies that guarantee same-day delivery is considered to be very lax. There are no formal security procedures or checks for air freight, space available shipments. I am also informed that certain security procedures have been overlooked or disregarded to expedite onschedule departures. These are holes in Canada's airport and airline security.
If we are to have adequate airport and airline security, then the entire security issue should be thoroughly addressed. Security must be the quintessential concern of the air travel industry, but we have to reconcile an approach which will keep passengers secure; one which is fair to long-time loyal employees in this industry; and a security check procedure that will protect the individual's right to privacy.
The priority should be given to those areas which are a definite threat to safety and security rather than scrutinizing the personal lives of employees who have served the industry and all Canadians loyally in past years.

The logic behind these murders was the Soviet program of "Russification" of Ukraine. This process deliberately attacked Ukrainian religion, culture, language, and heritage, with the ultimate goal of eliminating all things Ukrainian. Similar atrocities took place in many towns and cities across Ukraine and amounted to deliberate cultural genocide.
The great famine of 1933 is a clear example of the viciousness of the Soviet regime against the Ukrainian populace. In 1933, in the process of collectivization, 7 million Ukrainian men, women, and children died, victims of a state-planned famine.
Many Canadians of Ukrainian origin have families in Ukraine who still suffer under the "Russification" program. They join with me in urging the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to exert all pressure possible on the Soviet Government to ensure fundamental human rights to the people of Ukraine, and to provide some measure of protection for cultural, religious, and linguistic rights of all minorities living under Soviet domination.

December 10, 1987

Mr. Speaker, there is a question on the minds of many Nova Scotians which must be answered. Will the Government of Canada act now to protect the fishery on the Georges Bank?
December 10, 1987

The Georges Bank is the most productive fishing ground in the entire North Atlantic. Studies of scallop stocks demonstrate that the growth of scallops on the Georges Bank on a yearly basis is far greater than that found on other banks off the coasts of the North Atlantic.
The Georges Bank is vital to the economy of Nova Scotia and contributes more than $300 million in value to the fishing industry, and accounts for more than 6,000 jobs.
I have stated in the past the view that there must be no oil and gas exploration on the Georges Bank. This rich fishery must be declared an environmentally sensitive area and protected as such. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext: When the House rose at 1 p.m., the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) had the floor.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose, I was speaking about the inadequacy of the process the Government has imposed upon Parliament and the Canadian people and the inadequacy of the time for debate and examination of the free trade agreement. I was speaking to a motion put by my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), which condemns the Government for the process as it stands and which calls on the Government to request a 60-day extension to the January 2 signing date so that Canadians, both those who are for and those who are against the agreement, can have time to take a good look at the text of it.
I was arguing that the time which remains to Parliament and Canadians between the time we receive the text, which will, I hope, be tomorrow, and the time of the signing of the agreement on January 2 is hopelessly inadequate. Given that there is a provision in the United States for Congress to extend the fast track, I cannot understand why it is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is unwilling to have the decency to request such an extension so the due parliamentary and political process can be followed.
If it is possible under the congressional procedure to have a time extension, why on earth would the Prime Minister who had given a commitment to full parliamentary and public debate not request such an extension? Perhaps 1 could understand it if there were no possibility of extending the date of January 2. 1 would still be angry with the Government for having put us in such a position. I would be angry with the Government for having negotiated with the Americans at the end of their fast-track procedure when they would have the natural advantage over us, because we would be in a position of having to conclude an agreement by a particular time.
The fact remains that the Prime Minister has not even tried. He has not requested or tried to see whether or not Congress and the President would allow for the possibility of such an extension. For that, the Government is to be condemned. That is why we have moved the motion condemning the Government, for not seeking that extension and for being satisfied
with a process that gives Canadians only a few weeks to consider the text of an agreement which will be some 2,000 pages long.
Part of this process has been the committee hearings. 1 had the dubious privilege of serving on that committee which travelled the country to hear witnesses, both pro and con, on the agreement. That process was completely flawed because the committee did not have the text before it; nor did the people from whom we heard. Many people who came before us supporting the agreement were only able to give conditional support. They would say that they support the agreement but they hope that this does not mean this and that does not mean that and that they need to see the final text. These people have thought through the agreement, want to see the final text and want to have an opportunity to render a judgment on that final text. However, they will not have that opportunity because of the time frame the Prime Minister has accepted for Canadian due process.
Looking for a silver lining in a cloud, I suppose that the committee hearings were not completely without value. They were awfully frustrating to the great many Canadians who were unable to come before us, but many of the people who came before the committee in support of the agreement, and there were just as many who were against it, were much more forthcoming and honest about the true impact of the agreement than we could ever get the Government to be.
The very best example of this that I can think of is the presentation of the former Premier of Alberta, Peter Lough-eed. Mr. Lougheed said openly and directly before the committee that under this agreement, provinces would never again be able to have a preferential pricing policy for domestic consumers or local industry. We have been trying to get the Minister of Energy (Mr. Masse) to say that in this House as clearly for months on end. We could not get the Government to be honest about the real impact of the part of the agreement which provides that there will be no discriminatory pricing.
Mr. Lougheed said to the committee that that would be the effect of the agreement and that he was glad of it. I am not glad of it. I think it will be a real disadvantage, particularly to provinces which have been able in the past to use preferential energy pricing as a means of attracting industry. Mr. Lougheed was at least honest about the effect of it.
Another example of this was the question of marketing boards and supply management. We have been saying since day one that this agreement would put at risk our supply management and marketing board system.
1 wonder if we could have some order, Mr. Speaker. It is a little hard to speak over the chuckles. I have the greatest of respect for the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, but if I cannot hear the jokes, I would prefer not to listen to the laughter.
December 10, 1987

We said from the very beginning that marketing boards and supply management were at risk as a result of this agreement. Every time we said that, the Government would say marketing boards are not on the table; the NDP is trying to create fear. The NDP is exaggerating. The NDP is this and the NDP is that. The Grocery Products Manufacturers of Canada appeared before the committee. I hope they cannot be accused of being part of the socialist hordes. They said things like you cannot have marketing boards and no tariffs. It makes no economic sense. Once you reduce tariffs, then you have to have either the elimination of marketing boards or a very fundamental change in them which would require farmers to receive a lower price than they do now for the products they sell to the association.
What is clear from that? Marketing boards are at risk. Exactly what we have been saying all along. That was said not by opposition Members but by the Grocery Products Manufacturers of Canada.
Every time we said social programs were at risk under this agreement we were accused of hysteria and trying to whip up irrational fears among the Canadian people. The irony is that the claim about social programs being involved was most validated in the evidence the committee received from businessmen themselves. Ironically, they brought it up.
I recall in Vancouver a member of the Business Council, I believe his name was Mr. Matkin, and on the other coast Mr. Cummings of National Sea, referred to the fact that one of the reasons investors sometimes locate a plant in Canada is because they find the social programs to be of benefit, not only to their employees but to themselves. Mr. Cummings said they had done a comparative study of their plant in New Hampshire and their plant in Nova Scotia. They found the Canadian plant was more competitive on balance. One of the reasons was that the plant in New Hampshire had to pay health care insurance for its employees, whereas the plant in Nova Scotia did not.
A similar point was made about how social programs become part of the calculus in determining what constitutes competitive advantage by some of the businessmen who appeared as witnesses in Vancouver.
The point is this. Whether we like it or not, social programs are part of the calculus. They are part of what is taken into consideration when we calculate competitive advantage. If we enter into a relationship with the U.S. in which we, over the next five to seven years, negotiate the meaning of a level playing field, it is absolutely inevitable that our social programs will come to be part of that debate. By entering into that agreement we will be creating a context in which arguments about social programs as part and parcel of what is calculated as competitive advantage will come about. Whether it is the argument I have just made about Americans saying Canadian social programs constitute a competitive advantage, or Canadian employers saying the tax burden they have to

I am trying to make this point-

A final point in the same vein. One of the things we said in the beginning was that a free trade agreement with the U.S. would mean the end of the Crow benefit in western Canada. It would be a further step towards dismantling the economic structures set up in western Canada over the years and which we value. We could not get the Government to say they were at risk but we saw a supporter of the agreement, the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association, and others, come before the committee and say yes, the Crow benefit is at stake. Not just the benefit being removed as a result of the agreement but the payment to the railways is at stake. This will lead to payment to producers and when you do that it means more trucking.
