I see my time is up. However, the fact remains that the only legitimate and final political process appropriate when a Government proposes to change the very nature of this country by entering into this comprehensive an agreement with our southern neighbour is an election. The sooner we have it, the sooner the Canadian people will be able to render their own judgment. That is absolutely necessary.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the comments of the Hon. Member. They were not rantings. I cannot use that word. However, I happen to disagree with them. I think they are causing unjustified fear among the public.
The Hon. Member talks about social programs being an unfair trade practice or tipping the scale in trade negotiations. I submit that if that is the case, why has it not been brought forward before now? The laws have been in place for that kind of an attack, as the NDP likes to put it, on our social programs. Yet it has not happened heretofore.
I know what the NDP are trying to do. They are trying to tie this into the trade talks, but it is just not factual. The trade laws on both sides of the border are basically the same. They come under the rules and regulations of GATT. The U.S. has had the opportunity to bring charges against Canada for

December 10, 1987
Supply
unfair trade practices if in fact they feel it is a distortion of trade, or places companies in an unfair competitive position. This has not happened and it is not going to happen.
Lowering tariff rates is not doing that at all. National treatment comes into play, as the Hon. Member knows. As long as all companies are treated equally and fairly, these will not come into play at all.
He talks about subsidies and transportation. That was another one of his theories. I can say to him that the agreement says very clearly that until all distortions to agricultural trade are on an equal basis, those particular subsidies will remain in place. The Hon. Member knows that. That has to do with trade with the U.S., not trade overseas or the shipping of any of our grain products overseas. There is a good market in the United States for certain types of our high quality grains. The agreement says that once we get on a level playing field, to use the current terminology, subsidies on both sides will be gone and there will be fair trade. We are talking about what is fair to both sides.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will have to keep my remarks brief because the committee which is drafting the report on the agreement is meeting right now and I need to be there. My understanding on the transportation subsidy is that the Crow benefit for Canola, for example, comes off right away rather than after everything else has been leveled out. We heard from the Canola producers and Canola oil manufacturers in western Canada that this would affect them right away.
With regard to the Crow benefit in general, I was talking about the effect this would have in the future. I did not make the claim which the Member alleged I made about it happening immediately.
I did not say that our social programs were an unfair trade practice. I do not think they are. I do not think they should have anything to do with trade. The Parliamentary Secretary talks about what has happened so far. I know what has happened so far. I am talking about what might happen as a result of this entirely new relationship. That which has happened so far is not a reliable guide.
The point I am making is that when you get into a levelplaying-field relationship these arguments will be generated. I am not saying that these arguments will succeed. I hope they will not. However, either the Minister is being very naive indeed or simply he does not want to admit that the arguments about social programs will become part of the negotiations. Over the next five to seven years we will be negotiating what constitutes a non-tariff barrier, what constitutes an unfair trade advantage of a non-tariff kind.
The Parliamentary Secretary says that he does not know how lowering tariffs can affect social programs. I am not talking about the lowering of tariffs. I am talking about the negotiations that will take place over the next five to seven
years about what the level playing field will look like. I think that is where the arguments will be generated about social programs.
I could be wrong, and I hope that I am. I hope I never get to find out. I hope we kill this deal, because I do not like it. However, if it does go through, and if what I am predicting does not come to pass at the end of the negotiating period, I will be one of the happiest guys around. However, if you consider the things that have been said you will see that social programs will become a part of the argument.
We know that the Americans already tried once to countervail unemployment insurance. They did not succeed, but I think they will have a better chance of succeeding under this arrangement. I believe the Government has gone into it "bass backwards" if you like. Before we get rid of all the tariffs we should have agreement on non-tariffs. We should have a standardization of social policies such as exists in the European common market countries.
I do not want standardization according to American standards. For the benefit of the American people I would like to have standardization according to Canadian standards so that they can have a medicare program like ours. However, I do not expect that to happen. If it does, it would be great, but history tells us otherwise. When you enter into this kind of a relationship, the weaker country tends to take on the characteristics of the stronger country.
We heard from a number of native people throughout the hearings who had something to tell us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext: They got before the committee?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Yes, they got before the committee on a couple of occasions. The Assembly of First Nations appeared before the committee here, the President of the Dene Nations appeared in Yellowknife, and Chief Moses Okimaw of Manitoba was part of the coalition. I am not pretending that they were not heard. I am saying that they had some advice for us.
They told us that they had lots of experience with treaties between themselves and very powerful institutions such as the Canadian Government. I see that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) is here, which is rather appropriate. The native people told us that in their experience it is the powerful people who interpret the treaties, who in the end have the leverage to say that the treaty means something other than what the native people said it did.
That is the kind of relationship into which we are entering with the United States. That was stated very well in Manitoba by Chief Moses Okimaw who was quoting from The Ecstasy of Rita Joe, I believe. He concluded by saying that free trade will make Indians of us all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in its motion put forward today the Opposition is asking us to extend the deadline for signing the agreement by 60 days. On the face
December 10, 1987

of it, that seems to be a reasonable request which anyone might wish to consider. It seems hardly likely that it could not be accommodated. However, the fact is that there are two reasons why it is an unreasonable request. First, it implies that extending the agreement would not jeopardize the agreement we have, that we could simply extend the deadline by 60 days and examine the agreement a little closer without having an impact on our ability to conclude successfully the agreement which we have reached. Second, the Opposition is suggesting to the House that we have not spent enough time considering the free trade agreement. If the Opposition were a little more aware of what has been going on in the country for the last five years beyond the assembly lines of Oshawa it would know that westerners have been requesting a free trade agreement for years. In 1911 this desire of western Canada was put forward. We were not successful at that time, but we intend to be successful this time.
The Official Opposition and the NDP know that liberalized trade has been on the national agenda for many decades and has come to the top of the agenda in the last 10 years. Our national economy and our standard of living depend upon our ability to sell the goods and services we produce. We sell our goods all over the world. Thirty percent of our Gross Domestic Product is comprised of exports. The United States is our largest trading partner by far. We must keep certain economic facts in mind when we consider a free trade agreement.
Within the entire organization of the OECD, Canada is second, after West Germany, in the percentage of our Gross National Product dependent on international trade. Canada is a trading nation. We have always been and always will be. The Opposition has forgotten that this free trade agreement must be placed within the entire history of our trade with the world. Trade is fundamental to us. Our country was founded on trade with the Hudson's Bay Company and the Northwest Company. The fur traders and voyageurs built forts, travelled this country, and brought settlers because we had things to trade.
We still have things to trade and we have examined ways in which we can continue to trade them. Free trade is one of those options. It has been studied by many people. I recall when Premier Lougheed of my Province of Alberta put this idea forward at a First Ministers' Conference. He envisaged this as the way the West, and Alberta in particular, could fulfill its true economic potential, by providing Albertans with an avenue into the American market. He also saw the threat of protectionism against those items we currently sell to the American market. He was at the forefront of that trade debate and brought this issue into the modern era.
The question of free trade has been studied by many groups, including economists, professors, bankers, and business people, as well as the federal Government and some provincial Governments. One of the most important of those studies occurred in the fall of 1982 when the former Government set up the Royal Commission on Economic Union and Development Prospects for Canada. It is more commonly known as the Macdonald Commission, and was chaired by the Hon. Donald
Supply
Macdonald, a former Minister of Finance under Prime Minister Trudeau.
That commission concluded that we must venture into untried ways that will demand open-mindedness, courage, innovation and determination. It went on to say that we must concentrate our efforts on obtaining secure access to the American market on which continental economic forces have made us increasingly dependent.
The Government has reacted to these challenges. We have been open minded and courageous. We have obtained secure access to the American market. Time and a series of international events have been on our side, such that we have been able to put this trade deal on the national agendas of both Canada and the United States. The Opposition is trying to ensure that free trade, and the state of the Canadian economy as a result of American protectionism fall to the bottom of those agendas.
We have spent years considering free trade and how it will affect us. During the 1977 to 1979 round of GATT negotiations, the Premiers of Canada expressed the view that, contrary to what the federal Government was then doing, there should be a two-pronged effort in Canadian trade initiatives, with a multilateral approach through GATT as well as on a bilateral basis with the United States. We did not do as well as we should have at the GATT negotiations because we are not part of a trading bloc like the European Economic Community, nor do we have the trading leverage of the larger nations like Japan or the United States. We did not have the empathy of the lesser developed countries and various other groups of nations in the world.
In 1980, Ronald Reagan sought election as President of the United States. One of his early commitments was to improve relations with his continental neighbours, Mexico and Canada. In 1983, the Macdonald Commission discussed the future of the Canadian economy through public hearings which were held throughout the country. It studied where the opportunities for job prospects might lie.
At the same time, the Ontario Economic Council produced a report by Mr. Harris and Mr. Cox which said that within Ontario there would be higher real incomes for Canadian labour and lower prices for many imported and domestically produced goods if we had a comprehensive trade agreement with the United States.
In 1984, however, the United States began to develop a trade deficit. This deficit developed for a multitude of reasons, including perhaps, an overvalued dollar. This, combined with a reduction in exports, caused protectionist Bills to spring up in the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate. This mood in the United States was increasingly threatening to Canada.
In January, 1985, the recently elected Conservative Government set forth three options for securing and enhancing access and export markets. The following month, the First Ministers met to discuss these options. One western Premier in particular, Peter Lougheed, was especially vocal in his support for a free trade deal.

In July, 1985, when the Macdonald Commission reported, its primary recommendation for economic policy was a comprehensive trade arrangement with the United States. This recommendation came from a group of people with the same political background as those who are now opposed to the deal.
Subsequently, the Prime Minister appointed a chief negotiator, Mr. Simon Reisman. The Premiers met to discuss provincial involvements during which there were several months of intensive negotiations. Throughout the course of negotiations, the Government consulted with advisory groups from various sectors of the economy. It met with industry representatives to discuss how particular tariff reductions would affect their industries. After numerous discussions and consultations, a comprehensive free trade agreement with the United States was made on October 3.
There have been a number of arguments against free trade presented in this House and elsewhere. Those arguments are wrong for a number of reasons, which I will outline later. Generally, though, they are wrong because they have neglected two factors.
First, those arguments neglect the fact that this is a trade agreement, not a political or cultural agreement.
Second, they do not recognize that this is a trade agreement which affects a number of sectors of the economy. The suggestions that our sovereignty will disappear or Canadians will no longer govern this country have extended the trade agreement to other spheres far beyond the scope of anything that this agreement does or contemplates doing. Those who say we will lose as a result of this deal have forgotten that this is one trade deal with one customer. We trade with other countries and hope to pursue liberalized trade with them in due course.
Let me give a brief outline of the basic aspects of this agreement which we signed with the United States. It is important to understand what underlies this agreement and how important it is to proceed without delay as has been suggested by this motion today. At the outset of the free trade talks, the Government stated clearly that a free trade agreement would be good for Canada or there would be no agreement. We have delivered on that commitment. On January 3, we will sign an agreement that is good for Canada.
Unlike the Opposition, our Government is not living in the past. We know that there is no status quo in the world trade environment, with rising protectionism in the United States and a changing world around us.
The events in the stock market last month demonstrated our vulnerability to world events. What happens in New York affects Toronto, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Zurich and London. We cannot insulate ourselves from the changing world around us. With today's information technology, business is conducted at paces never envisioned 25 years ago. Capital is moved around the world at the speed of light. In this environment, no country
can shield itself behind a wall of protectionism and try to insulate itself from world forces. We cannot return to the days of 50 years ago when every small village and town had a bakery, butcher shop, livery barn and blacksmith shop. Today, we cannot insulate ourselves from continuing change and from moving ahead into the future.
Every recognized study of this issue has concluded that the free trade agreement will be positive for the Canadian economy. These studies include those by the Economic Council of Canada, the C. D. Howe Institute-generally believed to be more of a Liberal-thinking research institute-the Canada West Foundation, the Fraser Institute, various banks, professional groups, professors and universities. Every single study of which I am aware concludes that this would be positive for the Canadian economy. No one concludes otherwise. We can rest assured that there are people around who are prepared to pay for studies to come up with the conclusions they want, but even the Ontario Government's study which was released yesterday indicated that this agreement would be a positive thing for the Ontario economy. We all know it will be positive for the regional economies. We all know Quebec is on side and agrees it will be positive for Quebec. And these studies also conclude that it will be good for Ontario.
Our industries operate in world environments, energy, agriculture and high technology. In the things we do, we are among the best and the most efficient in the world. We already trade in international markets. So what are the implications of this agreement? There will be lower prices for consumers as tariffs come down. For consumers, tariffs are a tax. They are highest on food and clothing, the very things on which people with lower incomes spend most of their income. If those tariffs are taken away, the standard of living is automatically increased for every Canadian.
The Economic Council of Canada has suggested a 5 per cent increase in the standard of living of Canadians. The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has suggested that in terms of setting up a complete household, the savings would be in the order of $8,000 per household. A study was done some years ago on the potential impact of removing tariffs on the poor. The study concluded that the removal of tariffs could put 25 per cent of the people currently living below the poverty line above that line.
We will be exporting goods and services to the United States, not jobs. There will be increased foreign investment in Canada. The economy will become more specialized, more efficient and more productive. Canadian firms will move to the frontier of technology and our society will become more outward looking.
Many members have heard of the slogan of the anti-free traders 75 years ago: "No truck or trade with the Yankees".
December 10, 1987

Those who echo that slogan today are, to quote Marshall McLuhan, marching backward into the future. This agreement reflects the confidence and determination of those who have a vision of a big Canada, big in prospects, big in opportunities, big in competitiveness, productivity increases and research and development.
This agreement is consistent with other agreements in the world. The European Economic Community has a more far-reaching agreement than is envisaged here. When Britain was considering entering the EEC, the same kind of arguments were put forward, that somehow the agreement would diminish the status of England as a independent country, somehow it would be less independent. But, as we know, that is foolishness. Britain is still Britain, the Queen is still the Queen, and Maggie Thatcher is still the Prime Minister and just as tough as ever. Smaller countries in Europe which have entered into the agreement agree it has been of great benefit to them. One will find none of those countries today that would withdraw from the EEC. None of those countries would give up the benefits that that trading arrangement has given to them.
Between Australia and New Zealand there is a trading agreement. These are two countries with relatively the same population differentia! as between Canada and the United States. New Zealand has benefited greatly from that agreement. All the economic theory indicates that smaller countries have benefited more than the larger countries because the smaller countries are the ones gaining access to the larger market.
In Canada we have a trade agreement with the United States called the Auto Pact. It was signed in 1965 by Prime Minister Pearson without consultation of Parliament. The same people who opposed that agreement are opposed to this one. Yet that agreement can be cancelled by either side on six months' notice. It is now the darling of those who opposed it when it was first brought in. Today the people who are the greatest benefactors of that agreement, namely the auto workers' unions, lead the opposition to the free trade agreement.
The City of Oshawa is the home of General Motors in Canada and is represented by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, known also as the Member for General Motors, which was built with $4.6 billion of foreign investment. Premier Devine has said he wants to take all the mayors from all of the towns and cities in Saskatchewan to visit Oshawa. He wants them to see whether all that foreign investment would be as bad for Saskatchewan as it has been for Oshawa. He said that all he wants is $4.6 billion for all of Saskatchewan. He will stop there. He is not greedy. That will be enough.
The free trade debate is really about two views of Canada. The first view is that we should protect ourselves from a too competitive world by using the state to prop up the inefficient and the uncompetitive. The other view, one in which we believe, is of confidence in our ability to compete in the world
Supply
as an outward-looking nation ready to take advantage of global opportunities. We firmly believe that Canadians will choose our vision of the future. Protectionism leads to depression and we must unite against that.
I want to examine for just a moment that other vision, the vision proposed by the Party putting forward the motion today that seeks to derail this agreement. I think it is worth while to consider for a moment the views of the New Democratic Party and, to a lesser degree, the views of the Liberal Party. Let us examine the New Democratic Party. On the national scene we have professors, high school teachers, community college lecturers, media types and so on. That is not meant to be negative about any of those people. We have plenty of them in the Conservative Party as well. But what the New Democratic Party does not have is balance. Those Members are long in the realm of ideas but short on experience. They have rarely managed anything, let alone an entire Government, yet profess to have the expertise necessary to tell all Canadians how to run their affairs. They do not have the confidence to trust Canadian initiative. They do not have the confidence in the ability of individual Canadians to compete in the world if they were just given the opportunity.
The NDP world is a world of ideas and commentary not the world of management. It wants to maintain the status quo. The NDP find solution in government intervention as a matter of first resort. That Party believes the free market should be interfered with whenever it threatens the present state of affairs. It spouts the cliches of outmoded protectionism. Protectionism is for those who have a small vision of Canada. The NDP is dominated by fear. It has neither confidence in itself nor a vision for Canada. New Democrats doubt their capacity to be Canadian without an artificial wall around them. They forget that trade has always been fundamental to our development as a nation, especially in western Canada.
I believe we must defeat this motion today. We must proceed with this agreement with dispatch. This motion would jeopardize the agreement that all of us from western Canada have worked so hard to get. I urge the House to defeat today's motion.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, the United States-Canada trade deal, falsely called the free trade deal, has raised more serious issues for Canada than any other measures submitted to Parliament or the Canadian people since the Second World War. Yet despite that fact, we are asked to deal with it as if it were a minor piece of legislation.
The manner in which the Government is trying to ram this measure through Parliament and past the Canadian people is totally unacceptable and contrary to all our democratic traditions. Not only are we meeting a U.S. fast-track timetable, a timetable which was made in the United States, but also under that timetable we in the Canadian Parliament will have much less time to consider this deal than the United States Congress.
The impact of this deal will be much greater in Canada than in the United States. For example, 80 per cent of our foreign trade is in the United States, while only 25 per cent of the United States foreign trade is in Canada. Yet our Government has submitted to a fast-track schedule for dealing with this matter which is against our interest.
The other thing for which one has to have complete disgust is the fact that it provides the American Congress, which is less interested in the deal, with more time to consider the measure than the Canadian Parliament. Not only that, but we have not yet seen the legal text of this agreement. We will be asked to approve it next week.
When the 35 page document entitled Elements of the Agreement was tabled in the House a short while ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated that we would have the legal text within three weeks. It is now 10 weeks, we are told that the legal text is finished, and we were told that we would have it today. We do not have it today. We are now told we may have it tomorrow, or perhaps we will have it on Monday. The House will adjourn on December 18, which is next Friday. We will be asked to debate, examine, and approve or reject this 1,200 page legal document in that short period of time.

December 10, 1987

Christmas and New Year's will come along and the break for the holidays, and the Prime Minister will sign the document on January 2. I do not know how anyone with any reason and intelligence can accept that something so important and with such far-reaching implications should be dealt with in such a summary manner.
I wish to refer to the United States system. Under the American Constitution treaties must be approved by the Congress, especially by the Senate. Under our Constitution in Canada, in law the Government need not submit a treaty to Parliament for its approval. The signature of the Government is sufficient to make that treaty legal. However, from time to time when something is divisive and controversial, and there appears to be a lack of consensus, Governments nevertheless have given Parliament a chance to examine the matter, debate it, and then decide on it. We know with the great majority of Conservatives in the House, that they will approve of it whether it is good or bad. But to deny the right to a full and complete examination and debate is totally unacceptable, as is stated in this resolution.
We are dealing with this free trade agreement which impacts on every aspect of our economic, social, and political life, and we are asked to do it in a summary way without having the total document. Compare that with the process we have with an ordinary Bill. The Bill is tabled for first reading, distributed, we all have a chance to look at it, then there is second reading debate, and a vote at the end of the second reading debate. The Bill is then sent to committee where witnesses are heard. The committee then sends it back to the House, there is a report stage with more debate and more possibility of amendment, and then there is a third reading debate and another vote. Then the Bill is sent to the Senate. Generally, those rules provide for a complete and thorough examination, but that is not happening with this so-called free trade agreement.
I can say as a member of the committee who examined the agreement-I hate to use the word "examined" because we were given only four weeks to examine with witnesses the Elements of the Agreement, two weeks in Ottawa and one day in each province and territory, except the Yukon-that at every meeting witnesses stated that they wanted more time to consider this. Even those who are in favour of free trade in principle stated that they had doubts, concerns, questions that they wanted answered, and they wanted more time. Not only professors and church people but business people came to the committee, such as people from the printing industry or the small printers in New Brunswick and the maritime provinces, and they wanted to look at the legal text of the deal to see how it impacted on their businesses. They were afraid that they would not have enough time to readjust their businesses to compete with large American firms. The demand for more time, more information, answers to questions, and concerns over what might and might not be covered were raised all over the country. Yet the Government is rushing this thing through as if it did not want us to know what is in it.
Why do we need more time? We need more time because this is a very complex, complicated deal which impacts on every phase of Canadian life, and seriously changes the type of country that we have. I know the members of the Government do not think that that is true, but many Canadians think it is true and they want time to look at this. Having been a member of that committee, I might say that when one reads something like this for the second, third, fourth and fifth time, one always sees something new. That is the benefit of a long debate and discussion. New individuals come to the committee with a new perspective that was not seen before. But that will not happen when it is rushed through in such a quick manner.
We are not dealing here with theoretical free trade. Some people are debating this issue as if we were at a university and discussing theoretical free trade or text book free trade. That is not what we are discussing. We are discussing the 35 page document, up to this moment the 35-page Elements of the Agreement signed between Canada and the United States on October 4. That is what we are discussing. Is that agreement a good or a bad agreement? We are not discussing theoretical free trade.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin) stated that this is just a trade agreement. All the members of his Party have been saying that wherever we went. But it is not only a trade agreement; it has serious implications for our political system and for our social programs. It needs close examination because of that.
What is in the 35 pages? 1 keep referring to the 35 pages, but God knows what will be in the 1,200 pages. At the beginning they stated it would be exactly the same as what was in the 35 pages. Then there was renegotiation of the shipping parts, the transportation parts, and now we hear something about postal rates. We will have to wait until we finally see the legal text. What is in the deal in itself requires much more examination than it has had to date.
Let us take a look at some of the things contained in the deal. If we look at the provisions on energy, I do not know how government Members can state that this particular statement with respect to energy is nothing more than a trade statement. It states:
There is broad agreement to assure the freest possible bilateral trade in energy, including non-discriminatory access for the United States to Canadian energy supplies . . .
If we look back at the political battle during the OPEC crisis in the seventies, if those were not political battles as well as economic battles, I do not know what political is. This is a sell-out of Canadian energy and resources to the United States. This is untrammeled access to Canadian energy supplies, or whatever it says. I just put it on record.
With respect to agriculture, our horticultural industry and many aspects of our farming industry are very, very upset and concerned about what it will do not only to the economics of
December 10, 1987

the farming industry but to a way of life-the family farm which is already in danger.
Turning to the Auto Pact, they said that the Auto Pact would not be included. However, we now find in the Elements of the Agreement that the safeguards have been taken away. The agreement removes any ability of the Canadian Government in the future, as long as the agreement exists, to screen or to bar foreign investment, even investment which it thinks is not in the best interest of the country. It outlaws "buy Canada" policies or government procurement policies which favour our own industry. If that is not political, I do not know what is, especially as an instrument of regional economic development. For the first time in the world we are including services in a trade agreement between countries. It has never been done before.
It also includes financial institutions. It changes the nature in which we deal with our financial institutions and with our cultural industries. We find that mentioned in the deal. All these things require a lot more discussion and examination than they have already been given, and it is not being done.
What did we get in exchange for some of the things I have just mentioned that we gave up, such as total access to our energy and putting Canadian agriculture which has a tough winter to deal with in competition with California, Florida, and Arizona in the southern United States where they do not have winters and they have very low costs? What did we get in exchange?
We are lowering tariffs over a 10-year period so that we will bring them down to a zero level. However, 80 per cent of the products which go between Canada and the United States are now tariff-free. By the way, because of that Canada had a $20 billion trade surplus with the United States just before the agreement was signed.
Until we went begging to the United States for this special arrangement, most Americans did not even realize that we had that big surplus with them. They thought the principal bogyman was Japan and they were aiming all their darts and arrows at Japan. Now they know that Canada must be dealt with as well. Of course, as soon as they knew, they started hitting our shakes and shingles, softwood lumber, potash, and many other industries.
In exchange for giving up all the things to which I referred, we got a lowering of tariffs from 20 per cent where there are still tariffs applicable. The non-tariff barriers still remain and, in particular, the right of the United States to apply countervailing duties and anti-dumping measures against us. This seriously impedes our regional development programs.
In our hearings in Atlantic Canada we referred to the fact that the American Department of Commerce had decided that 12 federal programs geared to assist the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada were unfair subsidies subject to countervail in the United States. They were such things as fishing vessel assistance programs, agricultural and rural development
Supply
agreements, economic and regional development agreements, fishing vessel insurance plans, industrial and regional development programs, and so on. In other words, the United States has reserved the right to countervail against programs, even programs that we in Canada might consider necessary to assist the lesser developed regions of the country. A lot more examination needs to be done in respect of those things in the deal.
What are the implications of the agreement for major matters not mentioned in the deal itself? Every time witnesses came to our committee and said that the Mulroney-Reagan deal undermined our sovereignty or restricted our political action, Conservative members of the committee would take out the Elements of the Agreement and say: "Where in here does it say that our sovereignty was threatened or undermined?" Of course it is not mentioned within the covers of this blue booklet. It is not mentioned there at all.
The same thing happened whenever witnesses would say that social programs, minimum wages, health and safety standards for workers, unemployment insurance, affirmative action, marketing boards, and environmental laws were threatened. Each time something like that was said, they would say: "Show it to us. Where does it say in this little blue book that those things are up for grabs?" Of course it does not say that in the little blue book, but it does not take much intelligence to conclude that when Canadian companies, which are subject to Canadian labour standards and to minimum wages and must pay check-offs for medicare and other things, compete with American companies, especially from "right to work" states in the south of the United States, they will have much higher costs in Canada and will not be able to compete.
This is exactly why the Grocery Products Manufacturers Association of Canada made representations to us. This is not the radical left. We heard from large companies. The President of Quaker Oats said that if we had to buy our raw material food products on the Canadian market, with all costs that are entailed, we would not be able to compete with American companies that can buy their products at much cheaper prices and with much cheaper overhead due to the fact that they have lower wages, lower social standards, and so on.
What happens when we have Canadian companies living in that regime and trying to compete with American companies? By the way, there has been a movement in United States manufacturing from the north to the south where those cheaper standards and lower standards exist. They even have-and it would take me a whole debate to get into it-this Mexican connection whereby American companies send products into Mexico to have them assembled at much cheaper rates and then send them back into Canada. In any case, what will happen is that there will be pressures to harmonize all our social and labour programs with those of the United States so that our Canadian companies will be able to compete, or Canadian companies will scale down their Canadian operations and open plants in the United States so that they can

December 10, 1987
Supply
manufacture at a much lower cost and still import or export into the Canadian market.
I would like to quote what a prominent German businessman said about this matter at a seminar on free trade in Montreal last weekend. The former chief of loans for the Dresden Bank said that without a free trade deal Europeans were almost forced to invest in Canada to reach the Canadian market, but that free trade would allow them to serve Canada from plants in the United States. He went on to say: "I know that is not a friendly argument but it seems to be the truth. If larger European firms are given the option of locating a manufacturing plant in either Canada or the United States, they will almost by definition choose the United States because of such factors as transportation costs, taxation rates, market size, and labour laws".
There is a lot more testimony if somebody wants to read it before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade on that very same matter.
There is pressure to harmonize or go to the United States. By the way, if that happens, a Canadian company which owns a branch plant in the United States to serve Canada will still make big profits. However, the workers in its Canadian plant will suffer because they will be laid off.
In conclusion, let me say that for a long time the Liberal Party has been in favour of liberalized trade. As a matter of fact, since the Second World War there has been a progressive reduction in tariffs between Canada and the United States, mostly accomplished through multilateral and sectoral arrangements. In those 40 years, Canadian tariffs came down from an average of 21 per cent to 9 per cent. United States tariffs came down from 32 per cent to 6 per cent. Right now, 80 per cent of the products that move between Canada and the United States are without tariff. Only 20 per cent of the products have some kind of meaningful tariffs. Because of the soundness of Canadian business practices, we have a $20-billion surplus with the United States.
Tariffs and other barriers to trade can be lowered without giving away our energy supply, without destroying our agriculture and without giving up our political control. We did it before in the 40 years since the Second World War and we can do it again.

Mr. Speaker, at this point in time when we just signed an agreement-the most important in this century-that will bring prosperity to all Canadians, men and women, and to all provinces, an agreement that will keep on ensuring prosperity across the land, I want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that having listened very carefully to the speech delivered by the Hon. Member from Notre-Dame-de-Grace- Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), I would like to know what his position as a Quebecer is on energy matters, since Quebec's
Premier welcomes this Agreement because of its impact on the economic development of the Province of Quebec, where energy is so vital.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a very easy question to deal with. We have not had a free trade deal for years and Quebec has been very successful with its energy and the export of its energy. We do not need this kind of deal to assist Quebec in the export of its electrical energy.
The problem with this deal is that in the opinion of many, and I admit it is divided opinion, this deal will prevent Quebec from having a two-price system under which it could charge lower prices for its own citizens or for industries as an incentive to establish in Quebec.
We all know that the aluminum industry in Quebec was established because of special deals between the electricity companies and the Government. According to Mr. Lougheed, the former Premier of Alberta, that kind of two-price system will no longer be possible even for electricity. If one price is charged in Canada, that is the price that will have to be charged in New York, Maine or New Hampshire. We will not be able to charge a high price down there and a lower price up here.
I will refer to the provisions of the deal again, because this is a very important question. I would ask the Hon. Member to look at the provisions in the document under energy where it refers to non-discriminatory access for the United States to Canadian energy supplies. Electricity is energy. It goes on to say that both sides have agreed to prohibit restrictions on imports or exports including quantitative restrictions, taxes, minimum import or export price requirements or any other equivalent measure subject to very limited exceptions. These exceptions include national security, times of war and short supply.
The point is that we will not be able to discriminate between sales made to Americans and sales made to Canadians or sales Hydro Quebec would make to an industry that would want to establish in Quebec. I think that that is a mistake.
I can understand Mr. Bourassa wanting to sell as much electricity to the United States as possible. I support that, but to accept this kind of agreement which ties his hands is another thing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. colleague about the manufacturing in Mexico to which he referred. If I have the figures correctly, I believe there are about 300,000 people in northern Mexico who work in plants that have been built by Americans. These people work at a very cheap rate of pay, 68 cents or 70 cents per hour American. These people will be able to make all kinds of products.
How does the Hon. Member, who was a member of the committee looking at the trade deal, see that affecting products produced here in Canada where there are higher
December 10, 1987

transportation rates and climatic differences? Does he see this as being an attack on certain industries in Canada?
Today, there are decent wage rates and social benefits such as unemployment insurance in Canada. Does he see this as an attack on the social net within Canadian society itself? Is this an indication that this agreement will assimilate Canadians to the American way of life, to American attitudes and to American high-pressure business at the expense of Canadian labour and competition?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is referring to what we call the Maquiladora Corridor, a corridor along the Mexican-U.S. border in which approximately 300,000 Mexican workers are now working in plants assembling parts made in the United States at wage rates much below those they would be paid in the United States.
For example, blue jeans are being assembled for $1 per pair in Mexico, whereas it would cost $7 per pair in the United States. This is not happening only to things like jeans but to refrigerators, stoves, video machines and a whole host of consumer goods like that.
Not only will that system hurt Canadians under this deal but it is already hurting many American workers who worked in plants in the northern United States. The American attitude is not one of intervening to protect the workers in the same way we traditionally do in this country. They are letting these American companies get away with it.
The trade negotiations office says that these products will not qualify under the free trade agreement for export to Canada without tariff. How will we be able to tell if a radio or a washing machine coming into Canada with an American brand name of an American company situated in the midUnited States did not have some of its components made south of the border under these kinds of arrangements?
The trade office says that there will be Canadian inspectors roaming all over the United States looking behind the panels of these products to see where their components are made and asking questions. With the deregulation in the United States and Canada and with the cut-backs in inspectors, I do not know how that will happen. Will there be massive armies of inspectors roaming all over the United States checking out these goods?
In any case, there is some dispute about this particular matter raised by my hon. colleague, and it is for this reason that these things should be given much more time. We should not rush through this debate in a few days. We should be holding hearings at least as long as the American Congress which, it seems, will hold hearings until next September. It does not even want to look at the deal in an official way until June.
Here we are, closing the whole debate next week sometime, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will sign it on

January 2. That is it for us. The American Congress will have time to look at all these things. We will not.

Member's contribution and it is my view that if there were a vaccine against exaggeration and inconsistency, it would now be in short supply in Canada because of the Liberal Party. They talk about regional economic development and say that some programs would be cut, reduced. I will spare you the list.
They talk about jobs. They talk about lost jobs, although the Economic Council of Canada and the Macdonald Commission-whose chairman, by the way, was not that much of a Conservative-made recommendations and reported very positive findings in that respect. Concerning the whole cultural aspect, Mr. Macdonald suggested among other things that whatever relates to popular culture is exempted from the provisions of the agreement. The Premier of Quebec and his predecessor on a number of occasions have given unconditional support to this day to the free trade agreeement with the United States, especially as far as Quebec's interest is concerned. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY-S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXTENSION OF DEADLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I personally believe that Mr. Bourassa gave his approval to this agreement too quickly. It is interesting to note how his Minister of Agriculture, in attending the meeting of I'Union des producteurs du Quebec began to hedge on this matter. It is also interesting to note that we had only one day of hearings in Quebec. We did not go to Quebec City, Lac-Saint-Jean, the Abitibi, or the Gaspe, just Montreal.
The eight groups that appeared before us in Montreal were divided. Four were opposed and four were in favour. Yet even those in favour had conditions. They had doubts in their minds. What we are discussing today is a motion by the NDP which says we are going at this thing too quickly. If the

agreement is good, it will stand up to intensive scrutiny over a period of time. The problem is that we are rushing at it too quickly. The Hon. Member does not have the legal text, and neither do I. Perhaps the Cabinet and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have it, but neither of us know what is in the legal text. If the agreement is as good as he says it is, let us spend at least as much time as the U.S. and really test it. Let us hear everybody.
It was only today that the Auto Parts Manufacturers Association said it is now opposing the agreement. It took that group this long and there are others that will take that long.
The Hon. Member referred to the Macdonald Commission and the Economic Council. Their studies were made before the agreement was concluded. They were done on a theoretical free trade model, not on this agreement. I repeat over and over again that we are discussing this agreement. Mitchell Sharp, a former Liberal cabinet Minister, said he was a free trader but is against this agreement. So is Eric Kierans. It is not a question of whether you are for or against textbook free trade, it is this agreement which is at issue.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate on the motion put forward by my Leader condemning the Government for rushing this trade deal through. Bishop De Roo of the Roman Catholic Church spoke of what he called the secretive fast-track deal the Government is rushing through. We are rushing it through on an American timetable which the Americans themselves are not going to follow. They have set the agenda, we are following it, and they are not going to follow it themselves.
The agenda does not leave adequate time for the people or Parliament of Canada to look at the agreement and see what is in it for them and what we are giving up. It does not allow us to engage in an important debate. President Reagan spoke of this as a new economic constitution for North America and we in this House should be able to look at the fine print and have the time to debate it. The committee should have the time to hear witnesses who have had time to study the document. The committee should not hold farcical hearings across the country where the witnesses have not had the final text to study. It spent a day in each province hearing from eight or 10 different organizations. The whole process from beginning to end has been a complete farce.
Horace Walpole once said this world is a comedy to those who think and a tragedy to those who feel. No doubt there are some who have no feeling for Canada as a nation. If they stand back and look objectively at what the Government has done, they should be able to appreciate the farcical nature of what is happening. For those of us who care about Canada, who have a sense of Canada as a nation in which we grew up and in which we want our children to grow up, a nation where we see a future, then this deal is a tragedy. The process is a tragedy and has to be condemned as such.
The process goes back to at least 1983 when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was seeking the leadership of the Progressive Conservative Party. At that time another person seeking to be the Leader, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), put forward a proposal for a comprehensive partnership with the U.S. When the present Prime Minister was asked what he thought about that proposal he said: "Canadians rejected free trade with the U.S. in 1911. They would do so again in 1983. Canada must increase its share of total world trade which has dropped by 33 per cent in the past two decades". I am quoting from Maclean's magazine of June 13, 1983.
The present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clarke), who was involved in the trade discussions, said: "Unrestrained free trade with the U.S. raises the possibility that thousands of jobs could be lost in such critical industries as textiles, furniture and footwear. Before we jump on the bandwagon of continentalism we should strengthen our industrial structures so that we are more competitive." The Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) said: "It's silly. Canada must improve relations and trade with the U.S., of course, but our natural destiny is to become a global leader, not America's weak sister". The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said: "Bilateral free trade with the U.S. is simplistic and naive. It would only serve to further diminish our ability to compete internationally".
We need to ask why these four people, all very influential in the present Cabinet, were opposed to free trade in 1983, and why they are attempting to foist off this trade deal on the Canadian people in 1987. If, as the Prime Minister said four years ago, Canadians would reject this deal, then why try to impose it on Canadians now?
I suggest one of the reasons they opposed it in 1983 was because there was still a substantial number of members of the Conservative Party who had some allegiance to the Diefen-baker heritage. Whatever faults John Diefenbaker had, at least he had a vision of Canada that went beyond Canada being just a branch plant of the U.S. I would like to read from his last speech as Prime Minister on February 5, 1963. He said at page 3441 of Hansard'.
Somebody said to me that if I take this stand then we are going to suffer danger in Canada, damage to Canada, and that we are going to do harm to Canada's economic strength. I do not accept that argument. It is an unworthy one.
-I cannot accept the fears of those who believe we must be subservient in order to be a good ally of any country in the world.
Macdonald fought this battle. The great merchants in the city of Montreal, in those days-not the French Canadians-had their views on this subject, that after all Canada would be that much stronger if it were joined with the United States. That was not Macdonald's view. That idea comes in with almost every generation.
I say this, Mr. Speaker. We are influenced in this way every day in our country on radio, television and in the press. When the leader of the United States speaks, we get it in detail over our television . . . .When I hear some saying that the fact that one dares to speak out will endanger Canada's economy, I wonder what the future of this country would be if those who have such fears and those who are of little faith held office in our country.
December 10, 1987

I believe in co-operation, in the closest co-operation, but not in the absorption of our viewpoint by any other nation. 1 believe in the maintenance in spirit and in fact of Canada's identity, with the right to determine her own policy without extramural assistance in determining that policy.
That was John Diefenbaker in 1963. It was that legacy to which the present Prime Minister felt he had to appeal when he was seeking to be the Leader of the Conservative Party. It is that legacy which he is betraying right now. The first people who were betrayed by this free trade deal were the members of the Conservative Party to whom the Prime Minister made commitments in 1983.
During the election campaign in 1984 the Prime Minister did not travel across Canada saying that he was going to strike a trade deal with Ronald Reagan. Instead, he talked about fair and honest government, open government. He spoke about the pork-barrel patronage that we had seen and were all fed up with. We have not seen open, honest government free from patronage. Instead, there has been a continuation of that and, in addition, the betrayal that is represented by the free trade deal which the Government is presently trying to push upon us.
Following the election in 1984 the Prime Minister proceeded to bring Canadian law into compliance with the desires of American business interests. Instead of a relationship of mutual friendship and respect there was a fawning subservience to the power of United States business. We saw the gutting of FIRA, the doing away with the National Energy Program, and the elimination, through Bill C-22, of decent pharmaceutical laws which allowed the production of low-cost generic drugs in order to satisfy the American pharmaceutical industry.
The Government allowed U.S. business to move into areas which it said it was going to protect. It allowed Gulf and Western to take over Prentice Hall book publishing. It is allowing Amoco to take over Dome Petroleum. All the time that we are making these concessions the United States is moving against vital Canadian industries. Yet the Prime Minister does nothing but smile and put his arm around President Reagan and sing with him.
While we were moving toward the trade deal the United States was trying to stake out an ever-wider territory in Canadian business. We saw the imposition of a 35 per cent countervail on shakes and shingles. The Government tried to maintain the other day that that had no real effect. However, Mr. Scott Clarke, a representative of the Independent Shake and Shingle Producers Association of British Columbia, appeared before the standing committee studying the trade deal last month. He supported the deal, yet he said:
As you are all aware, our industry was hit with a 35 per cent tariff on June 6, 1986. Prior to that date, our industry was a free trader. Since the inception of the tariff, our industry has seen curtailment in production, loss of jobs, and an increased failure rate among producers. In addition, some of my family's operations, along with our fellow competitors', have been forced to close down in Canada and relocate in the U.S.
Supply
Later, when asked, Mr. Clarke estimated that approximately 1,000 jobs had been lost in the Canadian shake and shingle industry because of that 35 per cent tariff.
We saw a 15 per cent countervail imposed on Canadian softwood lumber which was later changed to a 15 per cent export tax. In order to change that export tax we have to get the permission of the United States. We surrendered our sovereignty on that issue. Because of that John Sereny, the President of Green Forest Lumber Corporation of Toronto, one of Canada's largest lumber wholesalers said:
It is cheaper to bring lumber to the Ontario market from the U.S. west coast
than to buy the product from British Columbia.
That is what that 15 per cent countervail converted to a 15 per cent export tax has done to our lumber processing.
An 85 per cent tariff has been placed on potash. A 6 per cent tariff has been placed on Atlantic groundfish. All of this is taking place while the Prime Minister is talking about his great friendship with President Reagan. He was negotiating the free trade deal with what he might call good faith but what Canadians who look at it with some objectivity would call naive simplicity, or perhaps naive complicity, while the United States was pushing us for every possible advantage.
If I were going to preach on this issue I would take the text from the Book of Jeremiah, the second chapter, in which Jeremiah describes the nation of Israel as "A wild ass used to the wilderness, in her heat sniffing the wind! Who can restrain her lust? None who seek her need weary themselves".
The lust of the Prime Minister to get a free trade deal is like a wild ass in heat sniffing the east wind, as Jeremiah said. The way the Government has made one concession after another is absolutely obscene. "Open for business" is the way the Government has described it. "Canada is available" is what the Prime Minister is actually saying.
In the meantime the Americans appealed to the GATT over Canadian export restrictions on unprocessed salmon or herring. This directly affects the jobs of 4,000 to 6,000 shore workers in British Columbia. It affects several small communities in British Columbia which depend upon fish processing plants. Last month the preliminary decision of the GATT panel came down and it went against Canada. The final decision has not yet been made. It will probably be made early in the new year.
We know that of 52 decisions made by GATT panels 45 have been accepted, five have been dropped by mutual consent, and only two have been overturned by a full meeting of the GATT. Therefore, we do not have a great deal of confidence that, having lost the early appeal to the GATT panel, we will succeed before the larger meeting.
In the past Canada had the right either to accept or reject a GATT decision. As we have a lot of regard for GATT and believe in that kind of process we have usually accepted GATT decisions. However, this decision, which prohibits Canada from putting restrictions on the export of unprocessed herring

December 10, 1987
Supply
or salmon, erodes our basic right to shape our own economy. It erodes our sovereignty. It takes away from our right as a nation to control our own economy. It is something we cannot accept. It is something we must reject.
Unfortunately, the preliminary draft of the free trade deal makes this impossible. I quote from page 11 as follows:
Both Parties have agreed they will not maintain or introduce import or
export restrictions except in accordance with the GATT, or as modified by the
Agreement.
We have given away the opportunity to accept or reject GATT decisions. We are now bound, by this agreement with the United States, to accept GATT decisions.
It is important to look at the nature of shore workers. They have a highly seasonal type of work. At times they work long and unpredictable hours, at times they work a lot of overtime, and at times they work only a few hours a day. Seventy per cent of the shore workers in British Columbia are women. Due to a whole series of struggles that they along with other people in the fishing industry have experienced, they are highly unionized and have a decent wage. In 1983, the average wage was $11.94 an hour.
Yet because of the short work year, where they work concentrated hours in a few months, the average income for women is between $8,400 and $13,900, or between $11,400 and $20,000 for men. These shore workers are asking why their jobs were not protected in the trade negotiations. Why are they thrown overboard to the American sharks that want to come in to take their fish, leaving them without their jobs and their communities high and dry?
The Government should have insisted that the United States withdraw this appeal to GATT before it went any further with the trade negotiations. A primary consideration should have been to protect the jobs we already have.
Not only did the Government not ask strongly enough to have this withdrawn, it allowed an agreement that confirms this GATT decision and takes away Canada's right to reject it.
Part of Newfoundland's hesitancy in supporting the free trade deal was that it traditionally had the right to insist on the processing of fish before they are exported from Newfoundland. Newfoundland insisted on having that right protected. That right was confirmed for Atlantic Canada when the Government was involved in developing the final text, which none of us have seen yet. Now Atlantic provinces can continue to have restrictions that would prevent the export of unprocessed fish.
However, we have a Premier in British Columbia who was standing on the sidelines and cheering the trade deal as the greatest thing since sliced bread. He either did not take the time to look at what is involved in the agreement as far as British Columbia workers were concerned or did not care. As a result, we have a situation in which Atlantic workers are given
some protection and British Columbia workers are thrown overboard to the sharks. Fish will be processed in Seattle or Bellingham by non union workers. What kind of level playing field is that?
I understand that companies will be insisting on a level playing field. What about a level playing field for the workers?
In conclusion, let me just say that before Atlantic fishing communities give their support to this agreement they should look at the effects of that 6 per cent countervail.
On page 21 of the Elements of the Agreement dealing with the dispute settling process, it states that the panel:
. . . would review, based upon the administrative record, final AD/CVD
orders to determine if an investigative authority of either Party made a
decision not in accordance with its law (including statutes, legislative history,
regulations, administrative practice and judicial precedent).
This panel has to look at the whole history, at the precedents and previous practice. In the decision that was handed down in Atlantic Canada, there were over 50 different federal or provincial programs that were declared to be unfair subsidies. These are now enshrined in this agreement as part of the material that any panel involved in the dispute settling mechanism will consider. The ARDA Program, transitional programs, economic regional development programs, interest-free loans, over 50 different federal or provincial programs that are named in this countervail will be part of that history. They are enshrined in this agreement as something the Americans can continue to appeal as being an unfair subsidy.
This has been a flawed process. A bad process does not lead to a good agreement. It was a secretive and fast-track approach. We are working on the United States agenda rather than developing it in terms of our own agenda and our own needs. The Prime Minister is following the American agenda, which is not in the interest of the Canadian people. I urge government Members to listen to their constituents who are unhappy and confused about this agreement. They are unhappy about the way it is being rushed through without giving due process so that different segments of the Canadian society can examine it and have an impartial say. I urge that the whole process be slowed down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on the Hon. Member's speech. This afternoon it was mentioned in the House that Mexico will be able to ship cheap goods to Canada. We heard comments about the climate and cheap labour in Mexico.
This question was raised at one of the committee meetings which had been held across the country, and was responded to immediately. Gordon Ritchie, Ambassador and Deputy Chief Negotiator, wrote to the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard), who is the Chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade. He explained to him fully that there is no way Mexico will be able to ship cheap goods to this country. I will provide a copy of the letter
December 10, 1987

to the Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins).
I have been a Member of Parliament for 15 years. There is no way that any Member of Parliament will be an authority on all subjects. One must do research and listen to the experts.
In November, 1982, the then Liberal Government appointed a royal commission to study the economic union and development prospects for Canada. Three years and $24 million later, the Macdonald Commission presented its report which overwhelmingly recommended that Canada pursue free trade with the United States. The New Democratic Party is suggesting that these people are wrong and do not know what they are talking. That is absolutely ridiculous.
In March, 1974, the Liberal dominated Senate standing committee on foreign affairs was appointed to study Canada-U.S. relations. Eight years and over 100 witnesses later, the committee presented its report which overwhelmingly recommended that Canada pursue free trade with the United States.
Members opposite talk about plunging into this agreement. That is simply not the case. It will be phased in over 10 years.
If members of the NDP are correct in saying that this is a terrible and disastrous deal, I do not understand why the Canadian Manufacturers' Association would be supporting free trade. They are the ones who will be affected and know more about it than I or, especially, the NDP.
In the November 1987 issue of The Canadian Manufacturer, the President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Mr. J. Laurent Thibault, stated:
The CMA supports the agreement and will continue to work closely with the federal Government to further improve the relationship with our most important trading partner.
He further stated:
It offers the opportunity of continued increases in our standard of living while removing many historical tensions between western and central Canada. Canadian consumers will be clear beneficiaries through lower prices and increased choice of goods.
These are responsible people who are in the business. They know what they are doing. Therefore, I will listen to them and support free trade. If we had received a document from the CMA saying it is going to be a complete and total disaster, I would have great difficulty in supporting this free trade proposal.
Mr. John Bulloch, a very responsible Canadian and businessman, has great knowledge of business affairs in this country. He is the President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. He stated recently that securing access to the United States market is essential to the long-term viability of Canada as a participant in a fundamentally changing world economy. This idea that we are going to sit still and do nothing is not going to work.

While appearing before the House of Commons Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade on November 3, 1987, Mr. Bulloch said that the main interest of small business in the trade deal is the removal of tariffs and non-tariff barriers. That will be done over a 10 year period. He questioned his membership of 41,789 owners of small and medium-sized businesses, and the result was five to one in favour. Am I going to tell Mr. Bulloch he does not know what he is talking about? Am I to believe that these 40,000 business people are all wet, that they do not know what they are talking about? That is just absolutely ridiculous. More than five to one predicted the impact would be either positive or neutral. Mr. Bulloch pointed out all the reasons why it will benefit Canadian business. If it is going to benefit Canadian businesses, manufacturers and all the rest, it is going to be creating more employment.
I will listen to the experts. I am afraid I cannot accept the arguments that I have heard from the New Democratic Party today.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a brief comment in response to the Hon. Member. First, he should know, as we all do, that some industries have expressed real concern about this agreement. As far as the Canadian Manufacturers' Association being in support, is concerned, it might be good for the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. What I was saying is that it is not good for Canadian workers. It is not good for the shore workers of British Columbia. It will not be good for the fisheries workers of Atlantic Canada. We can look at a number of industries right across Canada and find the same thing.
The Hon. Member for Yellowhead said in 1983 that it was not going to be good for textile and furniture workers. I would like to read from the well-known Conservative George Grant who wrote Lament for a Nation. He said:
Capitalism is, after all, a way of life based on the principle that the most important activity is profit-making. That activity led the wealthy in the direction of continentalism. They lost nothing essential to the principle of their lives in losing their country. It is this very fact that has made capitalism the great solvent of all tradition in the modern era. When everything is made relative to profit making, all traditions of virtue are dissolved, including that aspect of virtue known as love of country.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a very brief comment with respect to the attitude the New Democratic Party assumes, which is virtually anti-American. I would like the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) to really put his case forward as to whether or not he feels we can compete with the Americans. I think if he really sat down and studied the Province of British Columbia, he would realize that the reason the 15 per cent export tax was placed on softwood lumber is that we were much too competitive for the Americans. The industry in the United States took action against our Canadian industry.
The Hon. Member spoke of Scott Clarke from Scott's Cedar Products. He cited the fact that there was an adjustment due to the 35 per cent tariff on shakes and shingles. He read from

December 10, 1987
Supply
Mr. Clarke's delivery before the standing committee, but he left out the fact that in the final analysis, Mr. Clarke, like everyone in the shake and shingle industry in British Columbia, whether cutting blocks or bolts or running saw mills, advocates and supports 100 per cent a free trade initiative with the United States of America.
1 think it is important that this be brought to light. I would like the Hon. Member to comment on Mr. Clarke's position. I would also like to point out to the Hon. Member that in a forum at which I was present in Vancouver with the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), a Mr. Bentley, who is head of Canadian Forest Products in the Province of British Columbia, clearly enunciated to the forum, to all British Columbians and to all Canadians that had we had the free trade arrangement in place, he felt there would be no 15 per cent export tax on lumber today because it would have been circumvented by that very agreement.
In conclusion, the Hon. Member cites the case of the B.C. shore workers. We are concerned about them as well. However, I think he is prejudging the situation. I have not seen the final draft, nor has he. Let us wait for the final draft on that particular issue.

Mr. Speaker, beginning with the Hon. Member's last comment about waiting until we have the final draft, the very point we are making over and over again is that the final draft has been delayed so long that the people of Canada are not going to have a chance to examine it in any kind of detail before the Prime Minister has signed away Canada's future. That is what we are concerned about.
The Hon. Member asked the question, can Canada compete? Well, I think any theory of free trade depends upon the concept of comparative advantage. Different countries will each do what they can do best. The question is, who decides what one country can do best? 1 believe it is the responsibility of the Government of a country to have some say over the economy of that country and to help to shape that economy.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: That is socialism in its extreme form.

That is not socialism. That is the sort of thing that is happening in Japan. That is what Sir John A. Macdonald wanted to do. He felt there should be a national policy. If that is socialism, we will baptize Sir John A. Macdonald and take him over here into the New Democratic Party and the Conservatives can forswear him. They have already forsworn his heritage of Canadianism. If the Hon. Member wants to say that Sir John A. Macdonald's policy is socialism, he can go ahead.
The problem with this trade agreement is that we are giving away our ability to shape our own economy. We are giving away our control over our energy resources. We are giving away our control over our fisheries resources. We are surrendering the comparative advantage that would allow the Government to make basic decisions about the strengths of this country. If we surrender everything in advance, as this
Government has done with the Americans, it is going to be very difficult to compete. If we are going to make all the concessions in advance, we are not going to be able to compete.
Finally, the Hon. Member commented on my statements regarding Mr. Clarke. I have made it very clear that Mr. Clarke was a witness who was in favour of the trade agreement. If the Hon. Member checks my remarks, I think he will find that. As for Mr. Bentley, the Head of Canadian Forest Products, I worked for him as head of Canadian Forest Products a few years ago. I did not have any great regard for the kind of attitude he had towards his workers.
